en: *The Intent of Roaming through the Avataṃsaka*, composed by the Śramaṇa Hu Jizang of Huiri Monastery.
Regarding the discourse on how this sutra came to exist in Jambudvīpa: although it is not recorded in the catalogs, the tradition maintains that Nāgārjuna...
There was a sycophantic disciple who urged his teacher to manifest his transformation alongside Śākyamuni, saying:
"Your wisdom and virtue are such that you ought to become a new Buddha.
Why be a disciple of Śākyamuni?"
He then acted according to what had been said, fixing a specific date and month to establish new precepts and new robes that were largely similar yet slightly different.
Seated within a crystal chamber, he contemplated this matter.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahānāga felt pity and compassion for him; he then took him back to his dragon palace, showed him the immeasurable sūtras of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and further showed him the sūtras of the seven past Buddhas.
During his ninety-day stay in the dragon palace, he read ten times as much as was available in Jambudvīpa; the titles of the remaining works could not be fully enumerated.

When Nāgārjuna departed from the dragon palace, the Dragon King presented him with this one section of a sutra for his departure. It was due to these circumstances that this sutra became available in Jambudvīpa.
Those who lecture on this sūtra in Jiangnan must also know its origins.
The three great Dharma Masters of the early period did not lecture on it, nor did Jianchu and Pengcheng do so in their later years.
During the evening lectures at Jianchu, [Dao'an] borrowed the exegetical commentary from Dharma Master Changgan.
During the evening lectures at Pengcheng, he did not permit others to ask questions about the texts not yet lectured upon.

Among the three great Dharma Masters of the earlier period and the two renowned virtuous ones of the later period, most did not lecture on this sutra; those who began to lecture on it started with [Hui]she at Mount She.

At that time, there was the eminent Dharma Master [Hui]sheng, who, acting as a donor (*dānapati*), engaged in the work of conversion and instruction. He attained more than three thousand understandings of the non-ordinary sutras, and over the course of seven occasions, he established eight assemblies. Beginning with the *Prajñā-vyūha* and concluding with *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, each assembly expounded the textual content of one specific scripture; at that time, the proceedings were truly magnificent and flourishing.
Later, Xinghuang succeeded to his legacy and greatly propagated these scriptures;
such was the manner of his lectures on the *Nidāna*.

However, the meaning of this sutra primarily opens the gates of the two Buddhas and the two teachings, as well as the Pure Land, the thirty mental stages (*triṃśac-cittotpāda*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), and so forth.
Now, the meaning of the Pure Land will be briefly elucidated.
There are generally four aspects to the Pure Land:
first, the principal teacher of transformation; second, the place of transformation; third, the gateway of teaching; and fourth, the assembly of disciples.
These four types are grouped into two pairs:

the transformer and the locus of transformation. These correspond to the two fruits of the Tathāgata—the primary and the secondary. The transformer is the primary fruit, while the locus of transformation is the secondary fruit; thus, they constitute the pair of the primary and the secondary.

The "pair of the teaching and its followers" refers to the teaching as the object-condition and the followers as the subjective condition; because the teaching is the object-condition and the followers are the subjective condition, this constitutes the pair of the teaching and its object-conditions.
Although there are four items, they are condensed into two points.
However, it is not only in the Pure Land that these four items exist; within each and every buddha-land throughout the ten directions and across the three periods of time, all four are fully present.
Although the lands of the three periods and ten directions are immeasurable, they do not exceed ten types of lands.
These ten types of lands are: first, pure;
second, defiled.
Third, the mixed;

fourth, pure in origin but impure in the end—originally a pure land, later, due to sentient beings of meager merit, that which was originally pure becomes defiled; this is called "originally pure, now defiled.
Fifth, impure in origin but pure in the end—the transformation toward [purity] can be understood accordingly.
This is the land of Śākyamuni, wherein five types of manifestations appear.
Furthermore, there are five other kinds, making ten types of lands in total.
All ten types of lands possess the aforementioned four characteristics; based on these ten types, which are grouped into two pairs, all lands are fully encompassed.
Among the ten categories, I shall briefly clarify the one concerning the Pure Land; within the four sections, I shall first distinguish the one concerning the Transformation Master.
Question:
Is this sutra spoken by Śākyamuni?
Was this spoken by Śākyamuni?

When the Great Master Xinghuang first expounded [this teaching], he immediately posed this question; however, in response to this question, there arose two interpretations: one from the North and one from the South.
The Southern School’s interpretation states:
Buddhism generally comprises three types—namely, the Sudden (Dun), the Gradual (Jian), and the Non-directional Indeterminate (Wufang Buding).
Regarding the Sudden Teaching: it refers to that wherein the teaching is entirely perfect and the principle is entirely complete, expounded for those of great capacity.
Therefore, a sutra states: "For example, when the sun rises, it first illuminates the high mountains. Hence, it is called the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao).

As for the Gradual Teaching (Jian-jiao), from its beginning at the Deer Park to its conclusion at the Crane Grove, the teachings spoken therein proceed from shallow to profound, being taught step by step; thus, it is termed the Gradual Teaching.
Within the teaching of gradual progression, there are five distinct stages.

As for what is called "unrestricted and indeterminate," it is such that advancing it does not reach the level of the sudden, yet retreating from it is not the gradual; because it follows conditions without fixed determination, it is called the indeterminate teaching.
Question:
Is this the Mahāyāna,
or is it the Hīnayāna?
The commentary states:
These are Mahāyāna teachings, such as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and the *Śrīmālādevī* sūtras.
The reason for employing these three sūtras is the desire to demonstrate that this [present] sūtra was spoken by Śākyamuni.
What is it? These three teachings are the Buddha’s teaching.
What kind of Buddha’s teaching is this?
The commentary states:
These three teachings exist from beginning to end throughout Śākyamuni Buddha’s single period of appearance in the world.
If this is the case, one can know for certain that the *Avataṃsaka* was spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha.
Although Śākyamuni taught these three teachings, they are nonetheless distinct from one another. Why is this?
If they are gradual teachings or non-discriminatory teachings, these are spoken for those present before him.

If this is the Sudden Teaching, it speaks of the people and flowers of that land from afar, similar to how Śākyamuni spoke from afar of the people and flowers of the Western Pure Land in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.
Just as there are three classes of people who attain rebirth in this land, so too is it with this sutra; this is Śākyamuni’s remote exposition of the pure lotus-treasury land and its inhabitants.
Next is the interpretation by the Northern Master.
That [Buddha] has three aspects:
first, the Dharma-body; second, the Reward-body; and third, the Transformation-body.

The *Avataṃsaka* is spoken by the Reward-body Buddha; the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and other sutras are spoken by the Transformation-body Buddha; the Dharma-body Buddha, however, does not speak.

He judged that Vairocana is the recompense-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) and Śākyamuni is the transformation-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya); Vairocana is the recompense of Śākyamuni, while Śākyamuni is the transformation of Vairocana, and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was spoken by the Buddha Vairocana.
This is how the two masters of the North and South have explained it.
Now, I shall critique the exegeses of these two masters and set forth the words of the Great Master (Asaṅga) in full detail.
Previously, I refuted the Southern interpretation that *kāra* and *śāstra* are not different; now, I again employ the same fourfold critique to show that they cannot be one.
First, the difference in the transforming masters:

the *Nirvāṇa* and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras were spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha; the seven locations and eight assemblies were spoken by Vairocana Buddha. This is because Vairocana is the fundamental Buddha (hon), while Śākyamuni is the manifested Buddha (jaku).
The *Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra* states: "I, Rocana, now sit upon the lotus pedestal; upon the thousand petals surrounding me, I manifest a thousand Śākyamunis."
Therefore, Śākyamuni is the manifestation (迹) and Śāna is the source (本).
If the source and manifestation were thus different, how could they be one?
Second, their places of transformation differ.
Śākyamuni resides in the Sahā world, while Vairocana resides in the Lotus Treasury World; the Sahā world is a realm of mixed evils, whereas the Lotus Treasury World is a land of pure purity.
Since the two locations are different, how could they be one?
Furthermore, when the Sahā world shakes, it does so in six ways, whereas when the Lotus Treasury world shakes, it does so in eighteen ways.
Furthermore, the two locations—the pedestal and the petals—are distinct: Vairocana resides upon the pedestal, while Śākyamuni resides upon the petals.
Since these two locations differ so greatly, how can they be considered one?
Third, there is a difference in their teaching methods:

Śākyamuni speaks of the three vehicles in a mixed manner, speaks of the partial and the full in a mixed manner, and speaks of the provisional and the ultimate in a mixed manner; whereas Vairocana speaks exclusively of the One Great Vehicle, exclusively of the Full, and exclusively of the Ultimate.

Śākyamuni responds to conditions of manifold diversity by teaching the manifold teachings; he responds to conditions of the three-in-one by teaching the three-in-one teaching; and so on, up to responding to conditions of both limited and unlimited by teaching the both limited and unlimited teachings.

Vairocana responds exclusively to the single great condition by teaching the single great teaching, and so on, up to responding to conditions of the fully perfected and unlimited by teaching the fully perfected and unlimited teachings.
If that were so, they could not be considered one.
Fourth, their retinues differ.

Śākyamuni possesses all three types—those with mixed objects, those with limited objects, and those with unlimited objects. For instance, the twelve hundred śrāvakas and bodhisattvas such as Maitreya constitute those with mixed objects.
The Śākyamuni alone possesses the great fulfillment of conditions, whereas Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and others possess the great conditions themselves.
Since the teachings differ, the conditions likewise differ.
Because the conditions differ, the two Buddhas cannot be considered one.
Using these four points as distinct arguments, the Southerners explain that the two Buddhas cannot be one.
Next, I shall further present the prior objection. Why is this?
He says: "Śākyamuni speaks of the Lotus Treasury World from afar, just as Śākyamuni speaks of the Land of Immeasurable Life while remaining here.
However, it is unknown who provided this interpretation."
The Master of Mount Zhong and the Master of Xinghuang both state:
This interpretation does not truly constitute a valid explanation, as its essential nature is not problematic; there is no need for further refutation. Why is this so?
Since you have already stated that Vairocana is identical to Śākyamuni, how can you say that Śākyamuni speaks from afar?
There is, however, another objection, which I shall now further set forth. What is it?
Śākyamuni taught the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* in two versions:
first, the *Contemplation Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, and second, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Contemplation of Infinite Life) was preached for Queen Vaidehī, the mother of King Bimbisāra; while the queen was in prison, she was instructed to practice the Buddha-contemplation samādhi.

If this *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* were preached for the sake of the sixteen virtuous monks, it would describe the purity of that land through the metaphor of human flowers, so as to enable those of the three grades in this world to attain rebirth despite their five pains and five burnings.
If that is so, while it is granted that the description of the Land of Immeasurable Life has a specific purpose, for what purpose does Śākyamuni describe the Lotus Treasury World from afar?
Since no such explanation is seen, one should not claim it is a remote description; the excellence of its substance need not be challenged.
Since the Great Master has already spoken these words, I shall briefly summarize their meaning.
This constitutes the first part: borrowing the Northerners' distinct criticisms to refute the Southerners.
Next, borrowing the Southerners' [criticisms] to refute the Northerners' distinct [positions], there are likewise two challenges.
He said: "Since these two Buddhas possess these four distinctions, how could they be one?
Therefore, the Huayan lectures in the North are superior to those in the South."
Now, this [objection] is refuted by employing the same four points as before.
First, the teacher of the transformation must not be different.

Regarding the three textual passages cited to refute the first point: in the "Chapter on the Names" (*Nāman-paṭala*) of this sutra, which belongs to the second assembly and was spoken by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, it says: "He is sometimes named Vairocana, sometimes named Śākyamuni, and sometimes named Siddhārtha."
Since they are both referred to by the name "Or," how can one say they are different?

If it were the case that because one is named Śākyamuni and the other is named Vairocana they were different, then because one is named "eye" and the other is named "organ of sight," they too would have to be different.
He poses a counter-question:

Second, the *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma* states, "Some see me as Vairocana; some see me as Śākyamuni. Since these are differences arising from the varying perceptions of sentient beings, how could the Buddha himself be different?
For instance, some may see the Buddha’s body as being three feet tall, while others may see it as boundless.

Just as the householder Ghoṣila saw the Buddha as short, yet the Great Brahmā King could not see the crown of the Buddha’s head—it is but a single Buddha, yet the perceptions differ according to conditions.

If one were to say that the two Buddhas are different because they are perceived as Śākyamuni and Vairocana, then they should also be considered different because they are perceived as long and short.
To counter-argue: if that were so, one should not say they are different.

Third, this sixth assembly of the sutra was preached in the Palace of Paranirmita-vaśavartin on the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages; Śākyamuni emitted light from the white tuft between his eyebrows to empower Vajragarbha to preach it.
Since it was Śākyamuni who exhorted Vajragarbha to speak of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), how can it be said that this was spoken by Vairocana?
If it were spoken by Vairocana, then Vairocana should have emitted light to offer his exhortation.
Now, this is Śākyamuni’s encouragement; therefore, one should not say that the two Buddhas differ so vastly.
Second, their locations cannot be different.

It is stated that this sutra was preached in the Kingdom of Magadha at the site of the Great Nirvana; Magadha is the same as Māgadha, which is merely a variation in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit—how could this concern any difference between the two?
If that is so, this sutra was still preached in the Sahā world.
How is this known?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "And the Great King Ajātaśatru of Magadha shall arrive before long, in a mere moment."
King Ajātaśatru is the sovereign of the kingdom of Magadha.
From this it may be known that the two places are not different.
Thirdly, the gateways of teaching must not differ.

What are they? Śākyamuni taught the miscellaneous teachings; Śākyamuni taught the purely pure teachings; Śākyamuni taught the half-and-full teachings; and Śākyamuni taught the purely full teachings. Among these, which are the purely pure teachings taught by Śākyamuni?
The commentary states:

Śākyamuni exhorted Vajragarbha to expound the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), which is contained within this very sutra; therefore, we know that Śākyamuni preached this purely sublime teaching.
Fourth, the retinue is likewise not different.
In the eighth assembly, the members of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna congregations are listed in full, including five hundred śrāvakas such as Śāriputra and Subhūti.
If that were so, the retinues of the two Buddhas would likewise not differ.

If it were claimed that Vairocana acts solely as the primary object of focus for one [retinue], then only the Mahāyāna assembly should be listed; why, then, are both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna assemblies fully enumerated?
If [the Buddha] acts, he must possess both great and small conditions.
Furthermore, since the listing is already mixed, these conditions are "mixed conditions" and this teaching is "mixed teaching.
Moreover, as for Śākyamuni’s great conditions—Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and so forth—there are no separate Mañjuśrīs or Maitreyas; how would they differ from Vairocana?
The minor disciples such as Śāriputra and Subhūti are not distinct from [the Buddhas] Śāriputra and Subhūti.
If this is the case, one should know that the retinues of the two Buddhas are likewise not different.
Since these four types are not different, how can you explain that the two Buddhas' modes of regulation differ?
This is the second specific objection. He says:

Vairocana is the reward-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) and Śākyamuni is the transformation-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya); Vairocana is the reward-body of Śākyamuni, and Śākyamuni is the transformation-body of Vairocana.
The Master [Daoxuan] raised an objection, saying:
"This would result in the mutual transposition of the two Buddhas, the overturning of the world, and the confusion of the teachings."

Regarding the statement on the mutual interchange of the two Buddhas: it means that Vairocana himself possesses both the recompense and the response bodies, and Vairocana himself possesses both the fundamental and the manifested traces; likewise, Śākyamuni himself possesses both the recompense and the response bodies, and he himself possesses both the fundamental and the manifested traces. How, then, can one point to that Buddha as this recompense body and this Buddha as that transformed manifestation, or point to that Buddha as this fundamental body and this Buddha as that manifested trace?

If one were to claim that the Buddha over there is the retribution-body (nirmāṇa-kāya) of this [Buddha here], and this Buddha is the transformation-body (nirmāṇa-kāya) of that [Buddha there], it would entail the error of two Buddhas mutually displacing one another.

As for the statement regarding the overturning of worlds: Śākyamuni himself emerges upon the petals of the flower, while Vairocana dwells freely upon the calyx of the flower; since these two worlds are each distinct, how could one point to the Buddha over there as the retribution-body of this one, or this Buddha as the transformation-body of that one?

Regarding the claim that this confuses the gates of the teachings: Śākyamuni responded to causes and conditions both great and small by preaching both Great and Small Teachings, whereas Vairocana preached the Great Teaching solely for great causes and conditions; how can one therefore take Vairocana to be the fundamental essence of Śākyamuni and Śākyamuni to be the manifested trace of Vairocana?
Previously, one borrowed the "other" to refute the "one"; here, one borrows the "other" to critique the "other.
To speak in general terms: previously, one borrowed the "other" of the North to critique the "one" of the South; now, one borrows the "one" of the South to refute the "other" of the North.
This concludes the mutual critique of the two schools' respective refutations of those two interpretations.
Having rejected both the "North" and "South" schools—both the "one" and "different" positions—as being incorrect, they then counter-interrogate:
"Since you have refuted both 'one' and 'different' as being incorrect, how do you provide your own distinct interpretation?"
The Dharma Master Jianchu once asked Xinghuang about this.
A great scholar there said:
"Are Śākyamuni and Vairocana one or different?"
He replied:
"Śākyamuni is Vairocana; Vairocana is Śākyamuni.
Jianchu then said:
I have understood.
How so? Since you speak of Śākyamuni as Vairocana and Vairocana as Śākyamuni, how could they be one and the same?
"How could they be different?"—by providing this single response, the other will immediately understand.
However, not only are "identity" and "difference" excluded; all four propositions are likewise negated.
Why is this? Śākyamuni is Śikhin; how could Śākyamuni be anything other than him?
This applies equally to the statement that they are not different.
Furthermore, is Śākyamuni identical to Śiva?
Is Śākyamuni distinct from Śiva?
Is Śākyamuni both identical and distinct, or neither identical nor distinct?

Although it is not [describable by] the four propositions of identity or difference, even when one wishes to speak of the four propositions of identity or difference, one does not lose the four propositions of dependent origination. Why?
For how could Śākyamuni and Sāṃkhyāna be one?
Not one, yet not losing oneness;
how could Śākyamuni and Vairocana be different?
Not different, yet not losing difference.
The same applies to the other two phrases.
Thus, it is not the case that there are no fourfold propositions (catuṣkoṭi), yet the fourfold propositions are not lost; this is because causes and conditions are unimpeded.
It is not the case that there are no fourfold propositions of identity and difference, yet the fourfold propositions of identity and difference both possess their textual expressions and meanings.
Why is this? The text states, "Sometimes named Śākyamuni, sometimes named Vairocana," and thus they cannot be considered different.
Yet, as the provisional and the real, or the origin and the manifestation, are distinct, they cannot be regarded as one.
Alternatively, for some who perceive through conditions that this is Śākyamuni, or for others who perceive through conditions that this is Vairocana, it is therefore both one and different.
Alternatively, for some who perceive through conditions that this is neither Śākyamuni nor Vairocana, it is therefore neither one nor different.
Therefore, because causes and conditions are unimpeded, there is nowhere they do not reach.
Nevertheless, one must first refute the four positions of others before the four positions of the present causes and conditions can be clarified.
Why is this? The words of others must also be examined; since their words are not correct, they ought to be scrutinized.
If their words are already [erroneous], why is it necessary to scrutinize them further?
The commentary states:
Although the words are correct, they do not capture the meaning of unimpededness regarding causes and conditions.
Since the meaning has been lost, the speech is not perfected.
Whether it be right or wrong, all must be refuted; only after refuting that [opposing] purity can one then clarify the present causal conditions without obstruction.
One employs these words in order to counter the "other house" (the opposing school) which has failed to realize what is not so.
Now, in elucidating the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), we do so solely to counteract their fixed definitions.

While those in the South maintain that [causes and conditions] are identical and those in the North maintain they are distinct, we clarify the identity and difference of the present causes and conditions in order to refute their fixed positions of identity and difference.
This statement answers the previous inquiry regarding identity and difference.
Next, the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) concerning identity and difference are further elucidated separately; alternatively, this may serve to establish the preceding point.
These four propositions differ from the four propositions traditionally used.
Regarding the four propositions: first, two Buddhas teach one doctrine; second, one Buddha teaches two doctrines; third, one Buddha teaches one doctrine; and fourth, two Buddhas teach two doctrines.

Regarding the two Buddhas who preach a single teaching: Vairocana and Śākyamuni are the two Buddhas; Vairocana is the fundamental (hon) and Śākyamuni is the trace (jaku). Since the fundamental and the trace, as well as the platform and the leaves, are distinct, they are therefore two Buddhas.
Regarding the "One Teaching": it refers to the One Teaching of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Since the *Nirvāṇa* is the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Avataṃsaka* is the *Nirvāṇa*, they constitute a single teaching.
Regarding "One Buddha and Two Teachings": "One Buddha" refers to the single Buddha who is both Śākyamuni and Vairocana.
Vairocana is Śākyamuni, and Śākyamuni is Vairocana, because the fundamental (hon) is the trace (jaku), and the trace is the fundamental.
It is said that although the fundamental and the manifest differ, they are one in their inconceivability; therefore, they are but a single Buddha.
Regarding the "two teachings," these are the two of the *Nirvāṇa* and the *Avataṃsaka*, which is why they are called the two teachings.
Regarding "two Buddhas and two teachings," this refers to the two Buddhas, Vairocana and Śākyamuni, and the two teachings, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Regarding "one Buddha and one teaching," this means that Śākyamuni is none other than Vairocana, and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is none other than the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
"What is this 'fourfold proposition'?
The explanation says:
it refers to the fourfold proposition of conjunction and disjunction.

"Two Buddhas and one teaching": this refers to separating the persons while unifying the teachings; that is, distinguishing between Vairocana and Śākyamuni as two, yet unifying the *Nirvāṇa* and the *Avataṃsaka* as one.

"One Buddha and two teachings" means that while the person is unified, the teachings are separated: Śākyamuni and Vairocana are combined as one Buddha, while the *Nirvāṇa* and *Avataṃsaka* sūtras are distinguished as two teachings.
"Two Buddhas and two teachings" means being separate from both person and teaching;
"one Buddha and one teaching" means uniting both person and teaching.
These four phrases are to be applied in this manner.
The reason for employing the four propositions is to answer the preceding question.
That previous question asked:
"Are the two Buddhas one or different?"
Now, looking at this fourfold response:
there are instances where two Buddhas preach a single teaching, and instances where a single Buddha preaches two teachings.

Regarding the two Buddhas preaching a single teaching: when Vairocana preaches the *Avataṃsaka*, he is preaching the *Nirvāṇa*; when Śākyamuni preaches the *Nirvāṇa*, he is preaching the *Avataṃsaka*.

Regarding "one Buddha and two teachings": what Śākyamuni taught as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is precisely what Vairocana Buddha taught; what Vairocana Buddha taught as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is precisely what Śākyamuni Buddha taught.
The remaining two phrases can be understood.
For this reason, it differs from the explanations of others.
The previous statement regarding "Śāna-Śākya" and "Śākya-Śāna" was made as a counter-argument against other schools; therefore, this present explanation is stated.
However, these words also have another meaning.
What is it? It is for the purpose of reading the sūtras.

The Sūtra states: "Vairocana is upon the pedestal, while Śākyamuni is upon the petals. This pedestal is the petal-pedestal, and these petals are the pedestal-petals; are the pedestal and the petals one and the same, or are they different?
It cannot be said to be identical, nor can it be said to be different; what, then, can it be named?
It is named the "leaf-by-leaf platform.
Just as it is with the leaf-by-leaf platform, so it is with Vairocana and Śākyamuni.
Question:
If the leaves of the pedestal become the pedestal and the flowers, and if Vairocana and Śākyamuni become one Buddha, is this so?
Explanation:
Question: What kind of Buddha is meant by the term "Attainer" (Tathāgata)?
When leaves and petals form a single flower, that flower is named a lotus.
When Vairocana and Śākyamuni become a single Buddha, what is the name of that Buddha?
The explanation says:
The petals of the pedestal form a single lotus flower, and Vairocana and Śākyamuni become a single manifested Buddha.
As the petals of the pedestal form a lotus flower, the lotus flowers share a single root;
as Vairocana and Śākyamuni become a single manifestation, the manifested Buddhas share one and the same source. This source is the Dharmakāya Buddha.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body.
Because they belong to the same realm, two Buddhas share the same root; it is like the stalk and leaves sharing a single root.
For these two reasons, it is said that Śākyamuni is Vairocana and Vairocana is Śākyamuni.
Next, the meaning of the mutual opening and non-opening of the two Buddhas is clarified.

Regarding "mutual opening and non-opening," this refers to the difference between the two Buddhas, the difference between the two lands, the difference between the two teaching gates, and the difference between the two assemblies of disciples.
Regarding the statement that the two Buddhas are distinct, both Śākyamuni and Vairocana each reveal their own fundamental and manifested aspects.
As for Vairocana revealing his fundamental and manifested aspects: Vairocana takes the Dharma-body as his fundamental aspect, while he himself serves as the manifested aspect.
The opening of the fundamental and the manifested by Śākyamuni is likewise so: taking the Dharma-body as the fundamental and Śākyamuni alone as the manifested.
The Dharma-body of Śākyamuni is the fundamental; Śākyamuni is the manifested.

However, within these manifestations (*jì*), one further distinguishes between the fundamental and the manifested; Śākyamuni is the fundamental within the manifested, while this very body further gives rise to other Buddhas, which constitutes the manifested within the manifested.
This is as described in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* regarding the acceptance of the offerings from Cunda and the great assembly.
Accepting the offering of Cunda represents the fundamental body within the trace;
accepting the offerings of the great assembly represents the trace within the trace.
Since this one instance is thus, other cases are likewise so.
Since Śākyamuni possesses these two layers of reality—original and manifested—Vairocana likewise possesses these two layers of original and manifested reality.
The Dharma-body is the original, while Vairocana is the manifestation.

Furthermore, within this manifestation, there is yet another distinction between the original and the manifested: not arising from the site of the path of tranquil extinction is the original within the manifestation; manifesting a body in the palaces of the six heavens is the manifestation within the manifestation.
Therefore, the two Buddhas possess two layers of origin and manifestation; this constitutes the principle that the two Buddhas mutually reveal one another yet do not reveal one another.
One must always speak in terms of causes and conditions; it cannot be explained in isolation.
Next, I shall clarify the non-opening and the opening of their characteristics.
The Dharma-body is the fundamental essence, while the *Sāmbhogakāya* (She-na) is its manifestation.
In terms of their essential nature, there should be only a single layer of fundamental and manifest.
Why is this? The Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*).
Just as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* appears for a great matter—namely, to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*), and so forth.

Furthermore, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Prajñā arises for the sake of a great matter; it arises for the sake of an inconceivable matter; it arises for the sake of a matter that is unequaled."

Now, Śākyamuni has appeared in the world solely for the sake of one great matter; he speaks of one great causal condition only for those of great capacity. Therefore, there can only be this [single] reality of fundamental and manifested aspects.
The true intention of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time should indeed be exactly like this.

Yet, regarding the manifestation within the traces (*jì*), one further distinguishes between the fundamental and the trace; this is solely because sentient beings in the defiled lands have heavy karmic offenses and dull faculties, being unable to endure the great transformation of Śākyamuni. Therefore, as a skillful means, one further distinguishes between the fundamental and the trace within the realm of the traces.

The "original" (hon) teaching is for those of great capacity in the Pure Land, explaining the great cause and great fruit; the "traces" (jaku) teaching is for those of dull capacity in the defiled land, wherein one first explains the gates of the Three Vehicles, next explains the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other teachings, and only thereafter can the Mahayana meanings of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* be expounded—just as in the parables of the burning house and the impoverished son.
At first, when beings could not be transformed by the Mahāyāna, he taught the three vehicles as a skillful means; only thereafter was he able to teach the Mahāyāna.

It is the same with the two Buddhas: because defiled sentient beings were unable to endure the great transformation of Vairocana, the Trace-Buddha further arose through skillful means, first teaching the three vehicles and later teaching the Mahāyāna.
For this reason, within the provisional manifestation (jaku) of Śākyamuni, the fundamental and the provisional are further distinguished:
Śākyamuni is the fundamental (hon), and Śikhin is the provisional (jaku). This is precisely the principle that two Buddhas do not open [one another], yet they mutually open one another.

However, although the primary and secondary manifestations (*honji-suijaku*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods throughout all time are immeasurable, they are fully encompassed by two phrases: "opening the manifest through the fundamental" and "not opening the fundamental through the manifest. For this reason, these two types are clarified.
Next, four propositions are established to clarify the preceding meaning.

These four propositions are: first, only the fundamental and not the phenomenal; second, only the phenomenal and not the fundamental; third, both phenomenal and fundamental; and fourth, neither fundamental nor phenomenal.
Where should these four phrases be applied?
These four phrases are used to establish the meaning of non-differentiation and differentiation; they must not be applied indiscriminately, for their application must be appropriate to the context.
Question:
Is it that there is only the fundamental (ben) and not the derivative (ji), or even neither fundamental nor derivative?
The explanation says:
That which is fundamentally real but not a mere trace is the Dharma-body;
as the Sūtra says, "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space.
That which is only a trace and not fundamental refers to Śākyamuni, who is merely the Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya).
That which is both the trace and the source is Śākyamuni.
From the perspective of the Dharmakāya, Śākyamuni is the trace; from the perspective of Śākyamuni [the historical Buddha], he is the source. Therefore, Śākyamuni is both the source and the trace.
"Neither fundamental nor derivative" refers to the synthesis of the preceding three phrases.
Why is this? Although there were three phrases previously, they are in fact comprised within the two phrases of "fundamental" and "derivative."

The Dharma-body is the fundamental; both Śākyamuni of the Saṃbhogakāya and Śākyamuni of the Nirmāṇakāya are manifestations. This fundamental is the fundamental of the manifestations, and these manifestations are the manifestations of the fundamental.
Without this fundamental, there would be no basis for the manifestation of traces;
without these traces, there would be no means to reveal the fundamental.
Without the fundamental reality (ben), there would be no way to manifest the traces; it is because of the fundamental reality that there are traces.
Without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental reality; it is because of the traces that there is the fundamental reality.
Because there are traces by virtue of the fundamental reality, the traces are themselves the fundamental reality and the traces.
Based on the trace, there is the fundamental; this fundamental is the fundamental of the trace.
Since the trace-fundamental is not the fundamental, and the fundamental-trace is not the trace, this is precisely the purity that is neither fundamental nor trace.
Thus, although the fundamental and the manifested differ, they are non-conceptually one; when unfolded, they pervade and fill the Dharma-realm, and when rolled up, they vanish without a trace.
This concludes the brief explanation of the Master of Transformation.
Now, the locations of transformation are distinguished. There are two such locations:
first, the Lotus Treasury World of Vairocana; second, the Sahā world of Śākyamuni.
One may also take the two previous Buddhas as a category for the two present locations, using the primary to illustrate the dependent. Why?
As stated previously regarding Vairocana and Śākyamuni, or Śākyamuni and Vairocana, they cannot be said to be one, nor can they be called different.

One cannot say they are identical, yet there are causes and conditions for their identity; one cannot call them different, yet there are causes and conditions for their difference. Therefore, while they are neither identical nor different, there are also causes and conditions for their identity and difference.
The present situation is likewise: the Lotus Treasury is the Sahā world, and the Sahā world is the Lotus Treasury; one cannot say they are identical, nor can one call them different.

One cannot say they are identical, yet they are identical by virtue of causes and conditions; one cannot call them different, yet they are different by virtue of causes and conditions. Therefore, while these two locations are neither identical nor different, they are also identical and different by virtue of causes and conditions.
This, then, establishes the basis for the categories;
here, the basis is correct.
Since the basis is thus correct, the same applies to the categories.

Why is this? This is precisely the relationship between the environment (*āśraya*) and the inhabitant (*āśrita*). Since the environment and inhabitant are thus, how could the inhabitant and environment not be likewise?
Therefore, while the two Buddhas and the two locations are neither identical nor different, they do not lose their causal relationship of identity and difference.
Next, taking the previous two categories of "origin" (*hon*) and "trace" (*saku*) and applying them to the present place of transformation, there are also two further points:
first, that each of the two lands has its own respective lands of origin and trace; second, that both places are discussed together in terms of their lands of origin and trace.

Regarding the discussion of the fundamental and trace lands for each of the two locations: as previously stated, within the locus of Vairocana, Vairocana’s dharma-body is the fundamental and Vairocana is the trace; furthermore, within the trace of Vairocana, the fundamental and the trace are further distinguished.

Now, the land is likewise so: where there is the Dharma-body of Śākyamuni, there is the land of the Dharma-body of Śākyamuni; where there is the trace of Śākyamuni, there is the land of the trace of Śākyamuni.
Within the trace of Śākyamuni, one reveals both the fundamental and the trace; thus, within the trace, one reveals the lands of both the fundamental and the trace.
As it is with Vairocana, so it is with Śākyamuni.
Question:
How is this performed?
The commentary states:
Vairocana possesses the realm of the Vairocana Dharma-body.
Question:
"What need is there for a land for the Dharma-body?
The explanation says:
"The land of the Dharma-body is precisely the true land."
Why is this? Because the True Dharma constitutes the Dharma-body, the True Dharma likewise constitutes the land; there is no difference whatsoever between this body and its land.

When the True Dharma is the body, it is called the Dharma-body; when it is that which the True Dharma relies upon, it is called the land. Therefore, the Dharma-body inherently possesses a pure and clean land.

Therefore, the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "The three classes of worthies and the ten stages of sages dwell in the retribution of their fruits; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
This refers exclusively to the Dharma-body Buddha dwelling in the pure land of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the statement that Vairocana constitutes the trace and that there is a land of the trace of Vairocana: therefore, at the beginning of this sutra’s first assembly, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva says:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This Lotus Treasury [World] is that which has been manifested by the power of the past vows of Vairocana."
"This land is the trace-ground (*vyañjana-bhūmi*) of Śākyamuni. Regarding this trace-ground of Śākyamuni:

as previously stated, his non-arising at the site of the tranquil and extinguished *bodhimaṇḍa* constitutes the fundamental reality (*mūla*), while manifesting his body within the palaces of the six celestial heavens constitutes the trace."
Other matters are immeasurable; I have merely clarified them by means of this single point.
Now, it is also possible to determine the lands of the original and the trace based on this same principle, though this interpretation is somewhat narrow.

Herein, I clarify the lands of the original and the trace within the trace-manifestation of Vairocana: the Lotus Treasury World (Padmagarbha-dhātu) is precisely the original land within the trace-manifestation.
Since Vairocana rules over ten oceans of Buddha-worlds, this is precisely the land within the traces of the traces.
Śākyamuni likewise possesses these two layers: as Śākyamuni has a Dharma-body Buddha, he must also have a Dharma-body land, which is no different from the Dharma-body land of Vairocana.
Why is this? The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share a common Dharma-body.
Since their Dharma-bodies are identical, there is likewise no difference between their Dharma-body lands.
The True Dharma constitutes the Dharma-body, and the reliance upon the True Dharma constitutes the land.
The land of Śākyamuni’s traces is precisely this Sahā world.
Regarding the land of the traces within the traces of Śākyamuni, it may also be understood according to the fundamental and the trace within the aforementioned traces.
Why is this? Receiving Cunda’s food constitutes the fundamental ground within the manifested realm (迹中本), and the Buddha is thus the fundamental land within the manifested realm.
Receiving the offerings of the great assembly constitutes the secondary manifestation within the manifested realm (迹中迹), and the Buddha is thus the secondary land within the manifested realm.
However, this matter is not singular, as seen in the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding Śākyamuni Buddha and his manifested Buddhas.
The land of Śākyamuni Buddha is the original land within the provisional realm (*jì*), while the lands of the manifested Buddhas are the provisional lands within the provisional realm.
Therefore, both Buddha-lands possess these two layers.
Next, it clarifies that the two Buddhas together discuss the lands of the fundamental and the manifested:
just as the Dharma-body is the fundamental and Śākyamuni is the manifested, there is only one fundamental Buddha and one manifested Buddha.
Furthermore, the lands of the Dharmakāya and the Sambhogakāya are exclusively the land of the single source and the land of the single trace.

The Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great matter; likewise, it is solely through the upright mind of the Sambhogakāya that the pure land is accomplished. However, because of sentient beings with meager merit, heavy offenses, and dull faculties, the land of the source and the land of the trace are distinguished within the land of the trace; thus, it becomes the impure land of Sahā.
Vairocana Padmagarbha is the original land within the realm of traces, while Śākyamuni Saha is the trace-land within the realm of traces.
Thus, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "I, Vairocana, now sit upon the lotus pedestal; upon the thousand petals surrounding me, I manifest a thousand Śākyamunis."
Within one flower are ten billion lands; in each land is one Śākyamuni. Thus, within these ten billion lands, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis.
The flower has a thousand petals, and upon each petal is one Śākyamuni; therefore, there are a thousand Śākyamunis.
On a single flower there are ten billion lands, and in each land there is one Śākyamuni; thus, there are a thousand times ten billion Śākyamunis.
Next, one should categorize the four phrases of "original" (*hon*) and "traced" (*jaku*) according to the lands of the original and the traced, which likewise comprise four phrases:
first, that which is only the original land and not the traced land, namely the land of the *dharmakāya*.
Second is that which is only a trace-land and not a fundamental land; this is the land of Śākyamuni.

Third is that which is both a fundamental and a trace land; this is the land of Vairocana, which is considered a trace in relation to the Dharma-body land, yet a fundamental land in relation to the land of Śākyamuni.
The fourth is the land that is neither fundamental nor derivative; it subsumes the previous three phrases.
Although there were three phrases previously, they do not go beyond the two phrases of the fundamental and the derivative.
The Dharma-body is the fundamental, while the two Buddhas, Śākyamuni and Vairocana, are the derivatives; this constitutes the derivative-as-fundamental and the fundamental-as-derivative.
Without the fundamental (hon) there would be no way to clarify the phenomenal (jaku); without the phenomenal there would be no way to clarify the fundamental.

That there is no fundamental without which the phenomenal cannot be clarified means that the phenomenal exists precisely because of the fundamental; that there is no phenomenal without which the fundamental cannot be clarified means that the fundamental exists precisely because of the phenomenal.
Because of the fundamental, the provisional is the fundamental;
because of the provisional, the fundamental is the provisional.
The fundamental is not the provisional, and the provisional is not the fundamental; being neither fundamental nor provisional is purity.

Since this is the case for the two Buddhas, the two lands may be understood accordingly; thus, the three phrases are subsumed into the phraseless, and the phraseless becoming phraseless is ultimate purity.

Although there are no phrases, yet within the absence of phrases there are phrases; thus, there are the phrases of the dependent and the primary, and the phrases of the original and the manifested. Consequently, these three phrases become two phrases, and these two phrases become the absence of phrases.
Now, that which is without phrases is a phrase; one phrase is immeasurable phrases, and for the sake of measurable phrases it is one phrase.
Immeasurable phrases are precisely one phrase—within the immeasurable, one understands the one.
One phrase is precisely immeasurable phrases—within the one, one understands the immeasurable.
To understand the one within the immeasurable is the "one within the immeasurable";
to understand the immeasurable within the one is the "immeasurable within the one.

That which is the immeasurable one is not simply one; that which is the one immeasurable is not simply immeasurable. Being neither one nor immeasurable, yet not losing the state of being the one immeasurable—these words are profound and subtle, and not easily heard.
Next, the meaning of the two lands being mutually open or not mutually open is clarified.
Generally, there are five kinds of lands:
first, the pure; second, the defiled; third, the impure-pure; fourth, the pure-impure; and fifth, the mixed land.
These five lands were elucidated by the Dharma Master Sengrui; these five lands comprehensively encompass all lands without exception. Why is this?
Because within a single pure land, there are immeasurable pure lands.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "There are ten billion asaṃkhyeya realms of pure lands: the lower-grade pure land of Amitābha in the west, and the upper-grade pure land of the World of the Striking of Sacred Robes."
Since the Pure Land is thus, one knows that the remaining four lands are likewise immeasurable.
This is why it is said that these five kinds of lands horizontally encompass all lands without exception.
Since the horizontal [classification] is thus established, the vertical [classification] is not fixed.
Among the five kinds of lands, we shall for now clarify the two lands of purity and defilement.
Within these there are immeasurable sets of four propositions; here, we shall first distinguish one such set of four propositions.

Regarding the four propositions: first, a single substance in a single location; second, different substances in different locations; third, different substances in a single location; and fourth, a single substance in different locations.

These four propositions are extremely difficult to understand; I shall now clarify them by reflecting upon Master Yingsheng’s interpretation of the Pure Land doctrine and the analysis provided by the Dharma Master of Guanzhong.
However, while the two phrases "a single substance in a single location" and "different substances in different locations" are easy to understand, the remaining two phrases are difficult to clarify.
First, let us ask:
what constitutes a "substance"?
If one asks what is meant by "conforming to the location" (*chù*), the explanation states:

"Substance" (*zhì*) refers to purity, impurity, and so forth; "location" (*chù*) refers to the spatial location. For example, a pure substance is in a western location, while an impure substance is in an eastern location.

Regarding the phrase "one substance and one location": there is one pure substance and one defiled substance. The one pure substance resides in the Western Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), while the one defiled substance resides in the Eastern Sahā world; therefore, it is said to be "one substance and one location."

Regarding the terms "different substances" and "different locations": when the pure and the impure are viewed in relation to one another, the pure substance differs from the impure substance and the impure substance differs from the pure substance; thus they are said to have different substances.

The location of the pure substance differs from the location of the impure substance and the location of the impure substance differs from the location of the pure substance; thus they are said to have different locations.
Regarding the phrase "different substances in one place" (*bhinnadravyaikadeśa*), this sentence is difficult to understand.
The meaning of "different substances in one" is also termed "the meaning of different substances being identical," which refers to difference and identity existing in a single location.
Furthermore, this clarifies that distinct substances may occupy the same location.
If one asks how it is that distinct substances occupy the same location,
the explanation is as follows:

Pure and impure realms of differing natures coexist within a single Sahā world; as in this sutra, the Lotus Treasury World exists within the Sahā world, and in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the Land of Wondrous Adornment exists within the Sahā world.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "While other multitudes see it consumed by fire, my Pure Land is not destroyed.
This refers to the pure substance existing within a defiled realm.
This briefly clarifies how the pure substance coexists with the defiled land in this manner.
Next, the question is asked:
"If one possesses a pure essence, can one still abide in a defiled land?
There are several meanings to be understood regarding this.
First, as for why a pure essence can exist within a defiled land: purity and defilement are without obstruction.
Because purity is unobstructed by defilement, the pure can exist in a defiled place;
because defilement is unobstructed by purity, the defiled can exist in a pure place.
Because they do not obstruct one another, the pure and the defiled can occupy the same location; the Elder Śikhaṇḍin Devaputra is cited as proof.
Śikhaṇḍin is a pure deva of the Form Realm who comes to the defiled realm of the Desire Realm without obstruction.
The Crown Prince Tianzi purifies the three realms within the triple world itself, yet he is not even obstructed by the defilements of the triple world;
how much less, then, would the Lotus Treasury Jewel-Adorned Land and others—which are not the triple world—be obstructed by the triple world?
The reason my Pure Land is not burned is that fire is the fire of the inverted three realms, and it can indeed burn the inverted three realms;
yet the Pure Land is not part of the three realms—how could the fire of the three realms possibly burn that which is not within the three realms?
Fire is a defiled fire that burns what is defiled; how could a defiled fire burn what is pure?
Therefore, my Pure Land is not destroyed, and it is always filled with devas and humans.
Furthermore, the Land of Jewel Adornment exists entirely within this Sahā world; one may dig and excavate the Sahā world, yet one does not dig or excavate the Land of Jewel Adornment.
What is this "digging"?
It is the digging of the triple world (*triloka*), which can only dig within the triple world.
The Land of Jewel Adornment is not the triple world; how could the digging of the triple world ever excavate that which is not the triple world?
If form returns to excavate form, how could form possibly excavate the subtle?
This is the interpretation of Master Shi; since ancient times, this interpretation has been criticized as follows:
From where did he obtain this interpretation?
This interpretation is the interpretation of Master Kumārajīva.

Master Kumārajīva was a master of the Three Treatises (Sanlun); according to the principles of the Three Treatises, one must "seize" from others. Therefore, it is possible for purity to exist within impurity.
Second, as for why this pure land exists within a defiled realm, let us instead question you regarding their coexistence. You ask:
"How could such a pure land exist here?"
Now, the explanation is given:
this Pure Land is produced by the pure karma of the Tathāgata; since the body of the Tathāgata is unimpeded, the land he brings forth is likewise unimpeded.

The body is itself the pure land of the environment and its inhabitants; that is, the pure environment and its inhabitants are an unimpeded basis. Because one realizes this unimpeded pure basis, it is likewise unimpeded.
Thus, because the pure [basis] is unimpeded, the land is unimpeded; and because it is unimpeded, it can exist even within a defiled realm.
Next, the question is asked:
"For what reason does the Pure Land exist within a defiled realm?

Having already explained the first two meanings for why the Pure Land can exist within a defiled realm, this now explains the underlying significance of the Pure Land being situated within a defiled realm.
Question:
For what reason does the Pure Land exist within a defiled realm?
There are two meanings for explaining this.

First, according to the intent of texts such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Vimalakīrti*, because one desires to transform and guide sentient beings, it is clarified that the Pure Land exists within the defiled realm.
The Pure Land is right here; for what reason do you not see it?
It is only because your merit is meager and your faculties dull, and because your mind dwells upon the views of annihilationism and eternalism that you fail to perceive it.
If one were to say that the defiled land is in the east and the pure land is in the west, one would be unable to transform sentient beings through one's spiritual influence.
Why is this? The Pure Land lies to the west and the defiled land lies to the east; these two worlds are separated by vast distances, so [the Pure Land] cannot be manifested here.

Now, the Way of the Pure Land is right here. It is because you harbor a mind of inverted views—clinging to permanence and severing the notion of impermanence—that you do not see it. You claim to abandon the false to preserve the true, and to discard the impermanent to grasp at eternal bliss. Because your mind dwells upon such things, it is impure; since the mind is impure, you do not see the Pure Land.

If one wishes to see the Pure Land, one must purify the mind; by eliminating such distinctions between the real and the false, or the permanent and the impermanent, when the intention is pure, it is called right contemplation. Because of this right contemplation, the Buddha-land becomes pure.
In order to transform these sentient beings, it is clarified that the Pure Land exists within the defiled realm.
Second, the reason the Pure Land exists within the defiled realm is to accord with what is perceived by those with whom one has affinities.
What does the Tathāgata do with the Pure Land?
It is not like a wealthy man who keeps precious objects stored inside his house; why would the Tathāgata use such a vast amount of pure land as a foundation?
Now it is clear that the Tathāgata takes this Pure Land as a skillful means to accommodate conditions.
Thus Master Zhao said:
"The Sage is empty and identical to the formless; how could his land have boundaries?"
The Holy Body has never existed, nor has it ever been non-existent; how then could there be a land or a non-land?
The Sage has never been like an image, nor has he ever been unlike one; he has never had a mind, nor has he ever been without a mind.
Never has there been "not-mind" apart from mind; mind arises from the existence of mind.
Never has there been "non-appearance" apart from appearance; appearance emerges from the existence of appearance.
Never has there been "non-appearance" apart from appearance; appearance and non-appearance accord with conditions, and conditions emerge from the existence of appearance.
There has never been a land that is not a land; whether it is a land or not a land is merely according to conditions.
There has never been purity or impurity; whether it is pure or impure is merely according to conditions.
If there are those who should be delivered through filth, he shows them earth and sand.
If one were to attain the Way through purity, it would manifest as precious gems and jade.
For this reason, the Pure Land exists within a defiled realm. Hitherto, it has been simply said that these two distinct natures exist in one place;
however, the underlying causes and conditions for why such purity and defilement—these differing natures—should coexist in a single location have not been understood.
This is because the explanation of "releasing" (the mind) carries this meaning.
Next, I shall clarify how a single substance appears in different locations.
While the preceding three phrases are still relatively easy to understand, this one phrase is the most difficult.
"How can a single substance exist in two different locations?
The explanation states:

"Another raises the case of a single substance, such as one pure substance existing in both the Western and Eastern lands, or one defiled substance existing in both the Northern and Southern regions."
Does this phrase exist, or does it not?
If it does not exist, then the four propositions cannot be established;
if it does exist, what is its referent?
Now, I shall clarify this single phrase through the meaning of number.
For now, let us examine it according to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
It is simply the single pure substance of Abhirati that appears in two locations: the East and the West.
Why is this? The single world of Abhirati was originally located in the eastern realm of Akṣobhya; Vimalakīrti took it up and brought it here to the western Sahā world.
If that is so, then it is simply the pure substance of a single Abhirati that has traveled between the two regions of the east and the west.
Just as it is with the pure land, so it is with the impure lands and others; therefore, this is a case of a single substance appearing in two locations.
As for the previous case of different substances in one location, the two substances of purity and impurity would then occupy the same place.
Now, just as a single material object can be in different locations, so too should a single pure object exist in two places simultaneously.
Let us now further explain this based on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
That sūtra states: "An inconceivable bodhisattva can take the Sahā world and cast it into another realm."

Without moving from his original position, he simply took up the Sahā world and cast it into the Western Land of Peace and Bliss; yet the Sahā world remained perfectly still. This may be called "reaching [the destination] without moving" and "moving there without moving."
If that is so, then this single foul substance passes through both the eastern and western regions; thus, it is one substance occupying two locations.
As it is with this foul substance, so it is with the other four lands by analogy.
Next, it clarifies that a single defiled substance exists simultaneously in both pure and impure locations.
Previously, it was explained that when a defiled substance is cast toward a pure location, that defiled substance passes through two locations;
now, it is clarified that a single defiled substance itself abides in both pure and impure locations at once.
Just as with the Sahā world within the Lotus Treasury, it is the single impure substance of the Sahā world that exists both in the Sahā location and in the Lotus Treasury location. Why is this?
A lotus is not constituted by its pedestal alone; rather, the flower and the petals together constitute a single lotus.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The pedestal, the petals, the filaments, and so forth, combined together form the lotus; the petals are not separate from the flower, for they abide within the flower."
Since the Sahā world resides upon the petals, it is known that the Sahā world is within the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha*).
Therefore, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "I, now as Vairocana, sit facing the lotus pedestal; upon the thousand surrounding petals, I manifest a thousand Śākyamunis."

Thus we know that the Sahā world rests upon the petals of the flower; since the petals do not depart from the flower, the Sahā world does not depart from the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbha-lokadhātu*).
If this is the case, the defiled land of Sahā exists not only within the realm of Sahā, but also within the realm of the Lotus Treasury.
Therefore, we know that this is a single substance existing in two locations.
Question:
How can it be that the Flower Treasury Sovereign Terrace and the Sahā World Sovereign Leaf are one substance existing in two locations?
The commentary states:
It possesses two meanings.

Sometimes it clarifies that the Sahā world and the Lotus Treasury World are distinct; the Sahā realm is situated outside the Lotus Treasury, yet because the pedestal and petals together constitute a single leaf, the Sahā world does not depart from the Lotus Treasury.
Why is this so? The explanation states:
it is intended to clarify that the Sahā world and the Flower Treasury World (Huazang) cannot be said to be different, nor can they be said to be one.
Because the two locations are distinct, they cannot be said to be one;
because they are not separate from one another, they cannot be said to be different.

They cannot be said to be one and yet one, nor can they be said to be different and yet different. This is thus neither one nor different, yet both one and different. A brief explanation of one type of tetralemma is as follows; now, let us further clarify and examine the meaning of these four propositions.
Question: Others also clarify these four propositions; how does your approach differ from theirs?
One cannot say that others lack these four propositions, for the sūtras and other texts fully contain this meaning.
He also elucidated these four propositions; what difference is there from the present analysis of these four?
The explanation is:
he was unable to clarify the meaning of these four propositions, whereas at this time one has finally attained the ability to clarify them.
Why is this? Although there are four propositions, they do not transcend the two propositions of identity and difference.
For another entity to be "one" with something else, it cannot be one by virtue of being different from it.
If there is difference that can be differentiated, it cannot be different by virtue of being one;
nor can it be one by virtue of being different. Oneness is oneness by its own nature;
difference is difference by its own nature. It is not different because of oneness, nor is it one because of difference.
If self-nature were one, then oneness would obstruct difference;
if self-nature were different, then difference would obstruct oneness.
Since difference already obstructs oneness, how could difference occupy the same location?
If difference cannot exist in the same location, then there is no unity.
Since there is no unity, how can there be difference?
Since neither unity nor difference exists, the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are not established.
It is merely like this when left alone;
if one attempts to grasp it, there is nothing at all. Why is this?
There is a unity that can be unified, yet this unity does not arise through difference;
there is a difference that can be differentiated, yet this difference does not arise through unity.
Because it does not arise through difference, unity is not established as unity.
Because it does not arise from oneness, difference is not established as different.

If oneness is not established as one, then there is no oneness; if difference is not established as different, then there is no difference. This is the absence of any discourse on oneness and difference; what four positions (catuṣkoṭi) could there be?

There may be one or there may be many; these constitute four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Since neither "one" nor "many" exists, the four propositions do not exist; therefore, others cannot clarify the meaning of the four propositions.
What is clarified here is that while there are no four propositions, they are nonetheless four propositions.
One must first clarify the meaning of the obstructive nature of others before one can elucidate the meaning of the non-obstructive nature of present causes and conditions.
Why is this? Now, there is not a single thing that is "one" by itself; it is "one" only because of difference.
There is no difference that can be differentiated; it is through oneness that there is difference, and through difference that there is oneness. Thus, by virtue of oneness, each thing is one;

by virtue of oneness, there is difference, which means that by virtue of difference, each thing is different. This may be called a phrase without phrases, two phrases within one phrase, and four phrases within two phrases.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The absence of a phrase-meaning is the phrase-meaning of a bodhisattva.
It is the same here: there is no phrase yet it is a phrase; one phrase becomes four, and four become no-phrase;
the four phrases are precisely one phrase, and that one phrase returns to being no-phrase.
When there is no phrase yet it is a phrase, that is not a phrase; when there is a phrase yet it is no phrase, that is not no phrase.
When it is neither a phrase nor no phrase, yet it is a phrase—this is the unimpeded phrase of a bodhisattva.
Because of the principle of unimpeded phrases (*asaṅga-pada*), one obtains such phenomena as a single substance existing in two locations or two substances existing in one location.
Therefore, the clarification of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) at this time differs from other [systems].

He cannot possess these four propositions because of the mutual obstruction between identity and difference: difference cannot exist in the same location, and identity cannot exist in a different location.
It is like two pillars obstructing one another; therefore, they cannot accommodate each other.
Why? Because a pillar is form (*rūpa*), and as for the explanation of form, it has the meaning of substantial obstruction (*sapratigha*).
A pillar is form; a pillar cannot contain a pillar.
Earth is also form; earth cannot contain earth.
At this very moment, there is no obstruction; because there is no obstruction, the one and the many can mutually exist within one another.
For this reason, others were unable to clarify these four propositions; it is only now that they can finally be distinguished.

Furthermore, while these four propositions are still relatively easy to understand in terms of their application to phenomena, the subsequent sets of four propositions will become increasingly difficult.
Next, another set of four propositions is further elucidated.
Having already completed the exposition of one set of four propositions in the preceding section,
we now clarify another set of four propositions that become progressively deeper and increasingly subtle.
However, regarding the four propositions mentioned previously, the intentions of various schools differ, and other treatises may either agree or disagree with them.
As for these current four propositions, not only do their intentions differ, but the treatises themselves diverge significantly.
Regarding the "four propositions," they are: distinct substance in one location, one substance in different locations, one substance in one location, and distinct substances in different locations.
As for "distinct substance in one location," it is called "distinct substance" because the pure and impure substances are different; this purity and impurity are due to causal conditions.
Regarding the purity and impurity of causes and conditions: there is no way to clarify impurity without purity, and no way to clarify purity without impurity.
Since there is no way to clarify impurity without purity, impurity is the purity of impurity;
since there is no way to clarify purity without impurity, purity is the impurity of purity.
If the defiled is pure, it is not pure; if the pure is defiled, it is not defiled. That which is neither defiled nor pure, where purity and defilement are non-dual, is called "one place.
Thus, while purity and defilement are two and distinct, that which is neither pure nor defiled, being non-dual, constitutes one place.
Regarding the phrase "one substance in different locations": previously, the two were not two; now they are called "the non-two as two.
Previously, purity and impurity were neither pure nor impure; now they are called "neither pure nor impure as pure and impure."

That which is neither pure nor defiled is called "pure" and "defiled"; this constitutes the non-duality of the one essence of that which is neither pure nor defiled, whereas purity and defilement as two are distinct locations—the reverse of the former case.

To speak of "a single substance and a single location" means that it is neither pure nor impure in substance, and neither pure nor impure in location; being non-dual constitutes the single substance, and being non-dual constitutes the single location.

Regarding the phrase "different substance and different location": it means that purity and impurity differ in substance, and purity and impurity differ in location; therefore, they are said to be of different substance and different location.
The Master’s primary intent lies in these four propositions.
Question:
What is the difference between these four phrases and the previous four phrases?
Explanation:

The previous four phrases were distinguished according to phenomena; now, although there are four phrases, they consist of only one phrase: "neither pure nor impure, yet pure, impure, pure-and-impure, and neither-pure-nor-impure.
This single phrase is expanded into four phrases, which is why it differs from the former.
Question:
Previously you spoke of substance and location, and now you again speak of substance and location; how do these differ from the substance and location mentioned before?
Explanation:

Previously, purity and impurity were taken as the distinct substances and the eastern and western directions as the locations; now, when it is said that there are distinct substances in a single location, purity and impurity constitute the distinct substances, while that which is neither pure nor impure constitutes the single location.

Purity and impurity are manifestly distinct, yet they are not non-distinct; purity and impurity are manifestly distinct, yet they do not cause the mind to move. They are dual, yet non-dual; therefore, two substances coexist in a single place.
Regarding "a single substance in different locations": that which is neither pure nor impure is taken as the single substance, while purity and impurity are taken as the two locations.
Regarding "a single substance in a single location": non-duality is taken as the single substance, and non-duality is taken as the single location.
Regarding "different substance and different location": the two states of purity and impurity constitute the substance, while the two locations of purity and impurity constitute the location.

Although there are four permutations, in the latter two cases the substance and location are identical to those of the former; thus, while the underlying intent remains the same, it is manifested differently. This, moreover, constitutes another set of four permutations.
Next, another type of fourfold set concerning impurity is clarified.
This fourfold set consists of: one substance and two views; two substances and one view; one substance and one view; and two substances and two views.
Of these four propositions, the first is difficult to understand while the latter three are easy to clarify.
For now, let us distinguish between a single substance and two views. What is this entity?
Furthermore, let us cite two sutras: the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Avataṃsaka*.
The *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* states that Śikhin saw gold and jade, while Śāriputra beheld only soil and sand.

In the eighth assembly of this sutra at the Jeta Grove Monastery, the great bodhisattvas saw the Jeta Grove as being composed of the seven precious jewels, while the five hundred śrāvakas saw it as having been constructed from clay and wood by Sudatta.
It is simply that because two conditions perceive a single substance differently, it is said that "one substance has two views.
Now I ask:
since the substance is one, what constitutes this substance as being one?
Is the defiled substance one?
Is the pure substance one?
Is the substance that is neither pure nor defiled one?
Regarding these three criticisms, there are three schools of interpretation.
First, the masters of the old *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* explain:
one is a pure basis and the other is a defiled basis.
With a body of pure substance alone, Śāriputra himself saw wood;
with a body of defiled substance alone, Brahmā himself saw gold.
It is the same with the Jetavana.
The *Dilun* commentary explains:

"A single substance is neither of the nature of gold nor of the nature of wood. It is like a forest tree: if it is grasped by a mind associated with conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), it becomes a tree of outflows (*sāsrava*); if it is grasped by a mind free from conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*), it becomes a forest tree without outflows (*anāsrava*)."

The tree has never been either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*); it is designated as with or without outflows only in accordance with the two types of mind [that perceive it].

Now it is the same here: the nature is never pure or defiled; it is simply that when one perceives through pure conditions, one sees purity, and when one perceives through defiled conditions, one sees defilement.
Furthermore, there are three masters of the Śāstra who, having not mastered the meaning of a particular school, observe this interpretation:
"It is neither gold nor wood in substance; it is through conditions that one perceives it as gold or perceives it as wood."
This substance has never been either gold or wood; Śāriputra himself saw it as wood, while Brahmā himself saw it as gold.
This is called "one substance with different perceptions.
For now, I shall challenge this [position], not to refute the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* or the *Dilun*, but to challenge the interpretation of the Sanlun masters.
Once the three arguments have been refuted, what remains will collapse of its own accord. Why?

Your substance is neither gold nor wood. When Śāriputra and Brahmā both see the same object—one as wood and the other as gold—is it that Śāriputra sees the wood while the wood is neither wood nor gold, yet Śāriputra sees it as wood and Brahmā sees it as gold?
Regarding the Brahmā King: is it that the "neither-gold-nor-wood" is distinct from both gold and wood such that Śāriputra sees wood while the Brahmā King sees gold?
Or is it that there exists a "neither-gold-nor-wood" separate from Śāriputra’s wood and the Brahmā King’s gold, which is why Śāriputra sees wood and the Brahmā King sees gold?
Furthermore, let us open these three critical points and raise successive objections.

If it is merely that the son of Śāriputra sees wood because it is neither gold nor wood, while Brahmā sees gold, then when the wood seen by the son of Śāriputra is burned, is the gold seen by Brahmā also burned or not?
Furthermore, two further points are raised to challenge this single statement:
