If Śāriputra’s body were burned by the wood and the Brahma King were burned by gold, then the law of karmic cause and effect would be violated. Why?

The evil karma of Śāriputra caused him to perceive wood, while the virtuous karma of the Brahmā King caused him to perceive gold; each of these two karmas produced its own respective result. Since Śāriputra’s karma was destroyed, the wood was naturally consumed by fire;
yet since the Brahmā King’s karma was not destroyed, how could his gold also be burned?
Furthermore, while the evil karma of Śāriputra may be destroyed, why should the virtuous karma of the Brahmā King be destroyed?

Since evil karma destroys [its fruit] and virtuous karma likewise destroys [its fruit], and since the destruction of hell likewise entails the destruction of heaven, it is not the case that Śāriputra’s wooden body is destroyed while the golden body of the Brahmā King should not be destroyed.

Furthermore, since wholesome karma is governed such that it cannot be destroyed, and as they share the same wood, how could their unwholesome and wholesome karmas—which are likewise governed—be destroyed?
Therefore, they cannot be destroyed together.
If it were the case that Śāriputra’s wood perished while the Brahma King’s gold did not perish, there would then be two substances; how could one speak of "one substance with two views"?

The former point establishes that if there is one substance, the principle of the destruction of karma is undermined; the latter point establishes that if there is the principle of karma, the principle of one substance is undermined.

If, in the case of the wood of Śāriputra, it is neither gold nor wood yet both gold and wood are seen, then by analogy, it should be understood that for the Brahma-king, the gold is likewise neither gold nor wood.

Next, regarding the claim that there is a single substance which is neither gold nor wood, distinct from gold and wood, and that two conditions lead to the perception of these two: if you are "neither gold nor wood," do you mean that you are not this very gold and wood?
Is it that you do not negate this gold and wood?
If you negate what is neither gold nor wood by negating this gold and this wood, then gold and wood together would constitute "neither gold nor wood."
If that were so, you would again be subject to the previous difficulty regarding being burned. Why?
Since they share a single substance, if the wood is burned, the gold must likewise be burned.
Furthermore, if they were to jointly establish a substance that is neither gold nor wood, then both individuals who perceive it as gold or wood would be mistaken.
This substance is not gold, yet since the Brahma King perceives it as gold, he is not mistaken;
this substance is not wood, yet since Śāriputra perceives it as wood, he too is not mistaken.
It is not wood, for Śāriputra saw the wood as having fallen;
it is not gold, for Brahmā saw the gold as having likewise fallen.

Since both cases are equally neither gold nor wood, yet you say that Śāriputra fell while Brahmā did not, then since both are equally neither gold nor wood, is it not the case that Brahmā fell while Śāriputra did not?
Why is this? Because they are equally neither metal nor wood.
If "neither metal nor wood" were not "not non-metal and not non-wood," then there would be something that is neither metal nor wood existing separately from metal and wood.
Since it is already apart from metal and wood, how can there be something else that is neither metal nor wood?
Furthermore, if there were something else that is neither metal nor wood apart from metal and wood, then three entities would result:
the two entities of metal and wood, and the entity that is neither metal nor wood as a third; thus, three entities would be established.
The Master said:
"In this way, when one pear is at the time of being two pears, it is neither gold nor wood;
yet when it is a single substance, it is the dual substances of gold and wood. Therefore, the principle does not hold."
The meaning of these four propositions is difficult to understand even with this first one; it has not yet been resolved.
Now, the latter three propositions shall be explained.
Regarding the second proposition, which states "two substances and one vision," there are three meanings:
Regarding the "two substances," these are the two substances of purity and impurity.

Regarding the "one view," purity and impurity are the causes and conditions of purity and impurity; there is no way to clarify impurity without purity, and no way to distinguish purity without impurity. Because of purity, one speaks of impurity; because of impurity, one designates purity. Purity is the purity of impurity, and impurity is the impurity of purity. Thus, pure-impurity is not impure, and impure-purity is not pure.
It is simply that purity and impurity are not [inherently] pure or impure, because one perceives duality as non-dual.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Regarding clarity and ignorance, the deluded call them two."
"The wise understand that their nature is non-dual.
This non-dual nature is the true nature; it is the same for black and white dharmas, as well as pure and impure dharmas. Therefore, these two substances are seen as one.
Second, regarding the two natures of purity and impurity in speech, the deeply practicing Bodhisattvas perceive both as pure.
Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All conventional truths (saṃvṛti-satya) become ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) for the Tathāgata."
Whether mundane or supramundane, all things are truly real to the Tathāgata;
likewise, whether pure or defiled, the Bodhisattva perceives them all as pure.
As it is said in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Preacher" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: "Whether sweet or bitter, whatever flavors reach the mouth of a Bodhisattva all become nectar."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "When a bodhisattva observes matters of worldly production and industry, there is nothing that is not Prajñā.
Third, regarding sentient beings of evil karma, whether things are pure or impure, they perceive them all as impure.
It is like hungry ghosts, who not only see fire in that place, but see even the waters of the Ganges as fire.
It is also like those who go to the Lion Kingdom (Sīhaladvīpa) to collect pearls: those with merit obtain the pearls;
those with little merit see the pearls as snakes. Not only do they see snakes as snakes, but they see the pearls as snakes as well.
For this reason, there are two substances and one vision.

Regarding the third phrase, "one substance and one vision," it refers to a substance that is neither pure nor defiled, and a vision that is neither pure nor defiled; this is the Middle Way, the true land. This true land is precisely the Dharmakāya.
The *Prajñā* and the *Nirvāṇa*—this Middle Way and True Land—have never been pure in the past, nor are they impure now; they did not exist previously, yet they do not cease to exist now.
That which is neither pure nor defiled, neither existent nor non-existent, is called the True Dharma Body (Saddharmakāya).
This very True Dharma alone can serve as a place of refuge; it is therefore called the Land of the True Dharma (Saddharmabhūmi).
By whom is this true land perceived?
It is perceived by those who are neither pure nor defiled; because it is perceived by such persons, it is said that "a single substance is seen as one.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "a single substance is seen as one": when there is a substance that is neither pure nor defiled yet appears defiled through expedient means, there is consequently a perception that is neither pure nor defiled yet appears defiled through expedient means.
As it is with the defiled, so it is with the pure.

Based on a substratum that is neither pure nor defiled but is purified through skillful means, there arises a vision that is neither pure nor defiled but is purified through skillful means; therefore, it is said that there is one substratum and one vision.

This clarifies that previously it was shown that the real and the expedient each have one substance and one vision; now it is clarified that the real and the expedient each have one substance and one vision.

As for the fourth phrase, "two substances and two visions," this refers to that which is neither pure nor defiled, wherein purity and defilement both function together and both manifest simultaneously.

As in the manifestation of a thousand Śākyamunis upon a lotus pedestal, Vairocana is the fundamental essence (hon) and Śākyamuni is the manifested trace (ji); they are neither essence nor trace, yet essence and trace manifest together. Likewise, they are neither pure nor defiled, yet both purity and defilement appear simultaneously.
Since both are simultaneously manifested and both are simultaneously perceived, it is said that there are "two substances and two perceptions.
Nevertheless, these terms refer to one another. Why is this so?

Question: The second phrase of the preceding section also takes non-duality as a single view, and the third phrase likewise takes non-duality as a single view; what is the difference between them? Answer:

In the second phrase of the preceding section, one views duality and non-duality together as two substances forming a single view. In the third phrase, one views that which is fundamentally non-dual as non-dual, forming a single substance and a single view. Therefore, it differs from the former.
Next, it is explained that there are four kinds of lands:
first, the defiled-pure land; second, the pure-defiled land; third, the defiled-defiled land; and fourth, the pure-pure land.
Regarding the "defiled-pure land," this refers to the purity and defilement resulting from causes and conditions.
What is meant by this? Briefly stated, Vairocana and Śākyamuni open up the two aspects of purity and impurity: Vairocana represents purity, and Śākyamuni represents impurity.

This purity and impurity are the purity and impurity of causes and conditions; there is no way to clarify impurity without purity, and no way to clarify purity without impurity. Therefore, purity is the purity of impurity, and impurity is the impurity of purity. Thus, Vairocana is the impurity of purity, and Śākyamuni is the purity of impurity.
As it is with the secondary fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), so it is with the primary fruit (*phala*).

Śākyamuni is the manifestation (*traces*), while Śamantabhadra is the source (*root*); these are the root and manifestation of cause and condition. Without the root, there would be no way to clarify the manifestation; without the manifestation, there would be no way to distinguish the root. The root is the root of the manifestation, and the manifestation is the manifestation of the root.
Regarding what is called a defiled land or a pure land, these are produced by the inverted karma of sentient beings.
Because sentient beings possess inverted, defiled karma, they bring about a defiled land;
because they possess inverted, pure karma, they bring about a pure land.
The first two lines refer to what is produced by the delusions of sentient beings.
Question:
While a defiled land is produced by the karma of delusion, how can a pure land also be said to be produced by the karma of delusion?
How can inverted karma result in a pure land?
The explanation states:

Although they are equally inverted, among these inversions there are degrees of gravity and lightness. Because the inversion is grave, one perceives a defiled land; because the inversion is light, one perceives a pure land.
Although they are equally subject to perversion, there are degrees of severity in that perversion;
although the lands are the same, the lands differ, for some lands are defiled while others are pure.

Likewise, although the sentient beings currently being transformed are equally subject to perversion, their perversions differ: there are those whose perversion is pure and those whose perversion is defiled.

Although the various Buddhas who previously manifested transformations shared the same skillful means (*upāya*), their specific applications of those means differed; there were skillful means that were pure yet defiled, and skillful means that were defiled yet pure.
Thus, while the lands possess these four types, there are likewise four ways of perceiving them:

perceiving a pure land through causes and conditions, and perceiving a defiled land through causes and conditions—this refers to the perception of defiled and pure lands by the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through their causes and conditions.

Due to the perception of purity and impurity based on causes and conditions, sentient beings perceive an impure land as impure and a pure land as pure; thus, because sentient beings have inverted views of impurity and purity, there are four kinds of lands and likewise four kinds of views.

Having not yet completed the explanation of the meaning of clearly perceiving pure and impure lands, one further distinguishes the four permutations regarding a single impure land: first, seeing the impure but not the pure; second, seeing the pure but not the impure; third, seeing both the pure and the impure; and fourth, seeing neither the impure nor the pure.
These four phrases are distinguished according to two locations.
As for "seeing the defiled but not seeing the pure" and "seeing the pure but not seeing the defiled," according to what locations are these two distinguished?
The commentary states:
Let us examine this by way of the Jeta Grove alone.

It is simply one and the same Jeta Grove; yet, the five hundred śrāvakas saw only the Jeta Grove established by Sudatta and did not see the Jeta Grove of the Dharma-realm. Because their offenses were heavy and their merit was meager, and because of their minds of annihilationism and eternalism, they saw the Jeta Grove as defiled, filled with hills, mounds, pits, and ravines.

It is precisely because the mind harbors notions of annihilation and permanence, or of high and low, that one perceives the ruins of Jetavana as a landscape of uneven earth, rather than seeing the pure land of Jetavana within the Dharma-realm.

Since this is the case, it is likewise with the remaining three; one perceives only the Jetavana of Sudatta and does not perceive the Dharma-realm Jetavana, one perceives only the enjoyment of Śākyamuni and does not perceive the enjoyment of Vairocana, one perceives only the assemblies of the Three Vehicles and does not perceive the assembly consisting solely of Bodhisattvas, and one perceives only the teachings of the Three Vehicles and does not perceive the gate of the single Great Vehicle.
Therefore, it is said that one sees the defiled and does not see the pure.

Seeing the pure while not seeing the defiled is the reverse of the former; as with the various bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī within the dharma-realm, they see the Jetavana of the dharma-realm and do not see the Jetavana of Sudatta.

The reason for this is that because the minds of all bodhisattvas are free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, they do not perceive mounds or ruins, but see only the Dharmadhātu Jetavana; they do not see the Jetavana of Sudatta, but see only the enjoyment of Vairocana; they do not see the enjoyment of Śākyamuni, but see only the assembly of great bodhisattvas; they do not see the assemblies of the three vehicles, but see only the teachings of the Mahāyāna; and they do not see the teachings of the three vehicles.
Therefore, it is said that one sees the pure and does not see the defiled.
As for the statements "seeing both the pure and the defiled" and "neither seeing the pure nor seeing the defiled," by what means are these two phrases further elucidated?
The commentary states:
This explains the excellence [of the Buddha] in terms of the lotus pedestal.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "I, now as Vairocana, sit upon the lotus pedestal; upon the thousand petals surrounding me, I manifest a thousand Śākyamunis."
Sāhaṃ is the trace and Vairocana is the source; the platform represents the defiled and pure, while the leaves represent the pure and defiled.

Great-practice bodhisattvas not only perceive the source and trace of Sāhaṃ and Vairocana, but also perceive the trace and source of Vairocana and Sāhaṃ; they not only perceive the purity and defilement of the platform and the leaves, but also perceive the defilement and purity of the leaves and the platform. This constitutes the simultaneous perception of both purity and defilement.
Regarding the reason for seeing them as a pair, the Master said:
"It is because of the two types of wisdom in the causal stage and the two bodies in the stage of fruition.
It is precisely because Bodhisattvas possess these two types of wisdom that they see the two bodies of the Buddhas."
Not only does one see the traces, but one also sees the source; not only does one see the source, but one further sees the immeasurable traces within those traces.
Since this is so for the manifestation, it is likewise so for the basis; therefore, it is said that one sees both the pure and the defiled.

"One who sees neither purity nor defilement" refers to those who transcend the two vehicles; not only do they fail to see the distinction between the trace and the fundamental aspects of Śākyamuni and Vairocana, but they also fail to see the distinction between the fundamental and the trace aspects of Vairocana and Śākyamuni. Furthermore, they do not merely fail to see the distinction between the defiled and pure aspects of the leaves and the platform, but they also fail to see the distinction between the pure and defiled aspects of the platform and the leaves.
The reason one does not perceive two bodies or two lands is that they lack the wisdom of non-duality.
Because Bodhisattvas possess the wisdom of non-duality, they perceive two bodies; since [the Buddhas] lack this wisdom of non-duality, how could they perceive two bodies?
Not only is the source not seen, but the trace is also not seen; not only are the source and the trace not seen, but the immeasurable traces within the trace are also not seen.
As it is with the body, so it is with the land; therefore, it is said that neither purity nor defilement is seen.
Next, based on the previous two lines, one asks about the latter two lines. Why?
Since it was previously stated that "Bodhisattvas see the pure and do not see the defiled," for what reason is it further said that "Bodhisattvas see both the pure and the defiled"?
Previously, it was stated that those of the Two Vehicles perceive impurity but do not perceive purity; for what reason, then, is it now said that they perceive neither?

To answer these two sets of four propositions, another set of four propositions is now opened up: first, knowing but not seeing; second, seeing but not knowing; third, both seeing and knowing; and fourth, neither knowing nor seeing.
Regarding the phrase "knowing but not seeing," this sentence specifically takes up the previous meaning of the Bodhisattva seeing purity and not seeing impurity.

Thus it is said that the Bodhisattva knows but does not see: the Bodhisattva knows that Śrāvakas, through their karma of inverted views regarding annihilationism and eternalism, have brought about a desolate and impure land, and he knows that they perceive this [impure] land as such.
As for the land of a Bodhisattva, because the Bodhisattva’s karma is pure and his mind is pure, he does not perceive what others perceive in that land.

It is like a Buddha who, knowing the evil karma of hungry ghosts, perceives fire; yet the Buddha does not perceive the fire as it is perceived by them. Thus, it is said that "knowing yet not seeing," which explains the meaning of the Bodhisattva seeing purity and not seeing impurity.

Regarding the phrase "seeing yet not knowing," it refers to those śrāvakas who see only the impure land of Śākyamuni, yet do not know that Śākyamuni is Śākyamuni-Saṃbhava, nor do they know that the impure is simultaneously pure; therefore, it is said that they "see yet do not know."
Regarding the phrase "knowing and seeing": the Bodhisattva knows that Śāna is Śākyamuni and knows that Śākya is Śāna; he knows that the fundamental is the trace and the trace is the fundamental.
To know that the fundamental is the derivative is to see the fundamental as the derivative;
to know that the derivative is the fundamental and the derivative is to see the derivative as the fundamental.

Since this is the case for the fundamental and the derivative, it is likewise for the pure and the defiled: to know that the pure is the defilement of purity, and to know that the defiled is the defilement of purity.
Once one recognizes purity and defilement, one immediately perceives purity and defilement.

Once one knows that the fundamental is the trace and the trace is the fundamental, and knows that the platform is the leaf-platform and the leaf is the platform-leaf—just as the platform is one while the leaves are many, one thereby knows that the fundamental is one while the traces are many.
To know that one is many ones, and to know that many are one-many:
to know that one is many ones is to understand oneness within the immeasurable;
to know that many are one-many is to understand the immeasurable within oneness, such that the immeasurable does not obstruct the one.

Within the immeasurable, one is understood; one does not obstruct the immeasurable. Though immeasurable, it is one; though one, it is immeasurable. The immeasurable is one, and the one is immeasurable.
The immeasurable is neither one nor many; the one is neither immeasurable nor non-immeasurable; it is neither one nor immeasurable, yet through skillful means (*upāya*), the one is immeasurable.
Question:

If the fundamental and the manifested are many and one, and one and many, without obstruction—such that the fundamental is one while the manifested is many—why is it not the case that the manifested is one while the fundamental is many?
The commentary states:
As previously explained, we now briefly distinguish between the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku).
Regarding "the fundamental is one while the manifested is many": the fundamental is one because it is the essence; the manifested is immeasurable because it follows conditions.

Furthermore, because the fundamental [reality] (hon) is based on a single great condition, it is one; because the provisional manifestations (jaku) involve differing conditions, they are immeasurable.
As it is with the Buddhas of the fundamental and provisional, so it is with their lands.
To know these lands of the original and the trace is to see these lands of the original and the trace.
As for the statement that one "does not know" and "does not see," there are generally three meanings:

first, regarding what was previously known, it means clearly knowing that the original is the trace-original and knowing that the trace is the original-trace; and seeing that the original is the trace-original and seeing that the trace is the original-trace.
Since the fundamental and the manifest are thus, so too are the pure and the defiled.

Now one knows that there is no object of knowledge and no seeing, yet the pure and the defiled are vividly present; yet one has never known the pure and the defiled. The pure and the defiled are vividly seen, yet one has never seen the pure and the defiled.

One sees purity and impurity as distinct, yet they have never been pure or impure; it is like the analogy of the Buddha’s shadow in a stone cave: from afar, the marks and signs appear vividly, but upon reaching the edge, nothing at all is seen. Therefore, it is said that one neither knows nor perceives them.

Next, regarding "the mental discourse that neither knows nor sees": the followers of the Two Vehicles do not know that the fundamental is the provisional, nor do they know that the provisional is both the fundamental and the provisional; they do not know that the pure is the defiled-pure, nor do they know that the defiled is the pure-defiled. They do not see the fundamental, nor do they see the provisional; they do not see the pure, nor do they see the defiled. This is what is meant by being utterly ignorant and blind.
Therefore, a simile is cited in the sutra:

"It is as if two people were sleeping together; one ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and beholds the groves, gardens, celestial maidens, and other such things, while the other remains oblivious, unaware, and unconscious."

It is the same for Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles regarding matters such as the fundamental and the manifested, or the pure and the defiled: while the Bodhisattvas know and see these things, those of the Two Vehicles are utterly unable to know or see them.

The reason I provide this explanation is that such statements exist within the sutras; I am now speaking in order to explain those sutras, rather than offering this interpretation because I have conceived some new meaning at this present time.

Regarding the third point, "those who speak of the mind do not know and do not see": deluded ordinary beings do not know the fundamental source, nor do they see the trace-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Śākyamuni, nor do they see the land of Śākyamuni.
Although there are four propositions, they concern three types of persons.
"Knowing but not seeing" refers to a bodhisattva in relation to a śrāvaka.
"Seeing but not seeing" should be distinguished as pertaining to a śrāvaka.
To both know and see is to be a bodhisattva;
not to know and not to see is to be a sentient being.
Not knowing purity or defilement, and likewise not seeing purity or defilement—this is another aspect of the meaning of this principle.

Previously, we clarified the four propositions regarding one substance being seen differently; three of these propositions have now been explained, while one remains difficult and unresolved—namely, the proposition concerning one substance being seen differently. We shall now address this in turn.

However, regarding the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Dilun* (Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā), which explain how different perceptions arise from a single substance (*ekadravya*), the reason for the various criticisms and numerous challenges raised previously is precisely because they maintain that there exists a single substance which can be perceived as one.
Because there is a single substance that can correspond to another single substance, one thus encounters various difficulties.
Now, it is clarified that this single substance has never existed within [the mind].
If such a single substance did exist within, then there would be something else cast upon it, whereby it could be subject to the objections of others.
Now it is clarified that there has never been a single substance.

To speak of a single substance while asserting diverse perceptions—without [distinguishing] the Lotus Treasury from the non-Lotus Treasury, the Sahā world from the non-Sahā world, the pure from the impure, or the defiled from the non-defiled—is precisely the Tathāgata’s true land.

It is neither a pure nor an impure land; the distinction between pure and impure lands arises from two conditions. The true land of the Tathāgata has never existed and never been non-existent, and it is neither pure nor impure. This is thus neither existent nor non-existent, neither impure nor pure. Not knowing how else to designate it, we provisionally name it the "Middle Way True Land," for it is the land of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the statement that there is "one substance and two perceptions": the Tathāgata’s true land is neither pure nor defiled; those with pure conditions perceive it as pure, while those with defiled conditions perceive it as defiled.
The true land is neither pure nor defiled, yet Śāriputra perceives it as defiled because of his own defiled karma;
the true land is neither pure nor defiled, yet the various bodhisattvas perceive it as pure because of their own pure karma.

It is also like the Jeta Grove, which is neither pure nor defiled: Śāriputra saw it as the Jeta Grove recorded by Sudatta, saw it as the hills and mounds of Sahā, and saw it as that used by Śākyamuni;
whereas the Bodhisattvas see the Dharma-realm as the Jeta Grove, see it as the Lotus Treasury World, and see it as that used by Vairocana.
Therefore, it is simply that the Jetavana has never been pure nor ever impure; one perceives it as pure through pure conditions and perceives it as impure through impure conditions.
Question:
Since the true land has never been pure or impure, yet one perceives purity and impurity through pure and impure conditions, are both purity and impurity not distortions?
The commentary states:
Both [the pure and the impure] are distortions. The true land is neither pure nor impure; it is because of inverted, defiled karma that one perceives it as impure.
The true land is neither pure nor defiled; it appears pure because of inverted pure karma.
Thus, both purity and defilement are inversions.
Although they are equally inversions, there are degrees of lightness and heaviness among them.
The heavy inversion consists in perceiving what is not pure as impure; the light inversion consists in perceiving what is not impure as pure.
Therefore, the true land is neither pure nor impure, yet due to these two conditions, one perceives it as either pure or impure; this is called "one substance with two perceptions."
Question:
With what intention was this statement made?
With what intention do you say that the true land is neither pure nor defiled, yet because of the perception of purity and defilement, there are two views regarding a single substance?
The commentary states:
This is to explain the sutra.
What is the intention behind this statement in the sutra?
The commentary says:
This is for the sake of responding to conditions. Why is this so?
It clarifies that the Tathāgata’s true realm is neither pure nor defiled; to perceive it as either pure or defiled is equally a perversion.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states, in general terms:
"One does not perceive a defiled land by relying on the Buddha’s wisdom."
One should also say:
"Not relying on the Buddha’s correct wisdom and vision, one purifies the pure land.
Question:
If one perceives impurity and does not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom, why would one who perceives purity also not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom?
The explanation says:
the true land is not impure; since perceiving it as impure already shows a lack of reliance on the Buddha’s wisdom, [perceiving it as pure likewise does].
The true land is not pure; yet to perceive it as pure is likewise not to rely on the Buddha’s wisdom.
Furthermore, the land is not defiled; to perceive it as defiled is a defiled perception, and since the land is not pure, to perceive it as pure is a pure perception.
If this were the case, then both purity and impurity would not depend upon the Buddha’s wisdom;
both purity and impurity would be mere views and both would be inversions.
To counteract these conditions, it is said that the Tathāgata’s true land is neither pure nor impure, for it is in response to the perception of impurity and the perception of purity.
Furthermore, the reason for clarifying that the true land is neither pure nor defiled, while perceiving it as either pure or defiled, is to address those who have come from elsewhere.
For those who have come from elsewhere, there is no such principle as a land that is neither pure nor defiled.
If it is a pure land, it both exists and does not exist: according to the Sarvāstivāda of the Hīnayāna, it does not exist; according to the Mahāyāna, it does exist.
Question:
Since there are already painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, can there be pure lands and defiled lands, or pure-and-impure lands?
The commentator explains:
There are three types of sensation (vedanā), but there are not three types of lands (bhūmi).
There are only pure lands and defiled lands; there is no land that is neither impure nor non-defiled.
For the sake of such persons, it is clarified that there exist both impure and non-defiled lands.
The Tathāgata’s land of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is neither impure nor defiled; yet, depending on whether one perceives a pure land or a defiled land, [the distinction arises].
It is for this reason that the principle of a single substance with two aspects of perception is elucidated.
Meaning must necessarily have its origin; if its underlying cause is not apprehended, then the meaning cannot be established.

Now, it is clarified that these words were spoken for the purpose of reciting the scriptures or in response to others; had there been no such intention, there would have been no need for this clarification, and thus, according to our school, there is no such doctrinal meaning [in the original text].
Question:
Regarding "one substance and two views" and "two substances and one view," how are they distinguished in terms of delusion versus awakening, and loss versus gain?
The explanation says:
If these two substances are seen as one, that is awakening.
Therefore, the previous explanation stated:
"Luminosity and ignorance are treated as two by the deluded."
The wise person thoroughly understands that nature is non-dual.
It is the same with purity and impurity; because the wise person realizes that there is neither purity nor impurity, this constitutes awakening.

If it were a single substance perceived in two ways, that would be delusion. Since the true land is neither pure nor impure, yet one perceives it as pure or impure due to conditions, perceiving it as pure or impure through such conditions is delusion.
To perceive duality as non-duality is awakening; to perceive non-duality as duality is delusion.
To perceive duality as non-duality means to see these very two as non-dual.
To perceive non-duality as duality means to see that which is non-dual as dual.
Therefore, the matters of delusion and awakening are as easy to turn around as one’s palm.
The deluded see duality; the awakened see oneness—thus there is delusion and there is awakening.
The awakened neither see duality nor see oneness; since the Sage is neither deluded nor awakened, this is the purity that is neither one nor two, neither deluded nor awakened.
Question:

When the earth is neither pure nor impure, yet due to conditions one perceives it as pure or impure, such that there is a single substance seen differently by different observers—is it possible for a single pure substance to be seen as pure by one and as impure by another, such that there is a single substance seen differently?
Wei also posed this question.
The explanation states:
"It possesses three meanings."
That which is neither pure nor impure in substance is perceived as either pure or impure depending on the conditions; this principle has already been explained previously.

Furthermore, it is possible for a single pure substance to be perceived as both pure and impure depending on conditions, or for a single impure substance to be perceived as both impure and pure; this is termed "different perceptions of a single substance."
What is the reproof? It is explained as follows:
according to the *Śārdūlakarṇa-sūtra*, the city of Śārdūla was constructed from the seven precious jewels; when Śārdūla saw a golden pillar, other people saw it as a wooden pillar.

If one perceives a wooden pillar upon a single golden pillar, this is the case where a single pure substance is perceived as either pure or impure due to conditions; this is termed "different perceptions of a single substance.
Just as it is with a single pure substance, the same principle may be understood to apply to a single impure substance.
Question:
When Māndhātṛ sees a golden pillar, others see a wooden pillar.
When Māndhātṛ conceals the golden pillar, do others still see the wooden pillar or not?
The commentary states:
There are both those that are seen and those that are not seen. Why is this so?
Just as one sees wood upon a layer of gold within the earth, yet once the gold is concealed by the earth, the wood is no longer seen;
and just as one sees the form of a snake upon a jewel, yet once the jewel is concealed, no snake can be seen.
Question:
If other people no longer see the wood once it has been concealed by gold, then the principle of the ripening fruit of destructive karma would apply.
Why, then, do they still see the wood?
It is because of those evil karmas that one sees wood; seeing wood is the fruit of karma.
Now that the gold is no longer there, one no longer sees the wood, which illustrates the principle of the destruction of karmic fruits.
The commentary states:
Inverted objects each have their respective domains.
Gold belongs to the realm of Māyā; because it is powerful within the boundaries of the Māyā realm, the Māyā-store conceals the gold so that other people no longer see the wood.
Regarding the term "seeing": this clarifies that although gold may be hidden within the wood-element (*dāru-dhātu*), one still perceives the wood.
Question:
If gold is absent yet one still perceives the wood, then the principle of two distinct substances (*dravya*) is established.
If they were of a single substance, then in the absence of gold, one would not perceive wood;
yet if one does perceive it, there must be two substances.
Furthermore, when wood is perceived upon gold, since the gold is absent, how could there be any perception of wood?
The commentary states:
Although one still perceives the wood, it is a single substance; although it is a single substance, one still perceives the wood.
On this point, the Great Master cites the "divine snake" as a metaphor for each case.
A person walking along saw a snake and immediately cut it open; inside the snake's belly were wine and meat.
From where did this snake obtain the wine and meat?
This snake is a divine serpent; because people offered wine and meat as sacrifices to the deity, the snake thus obtained the wine and meat.
This wine and meat are the wine and meat of a person; though a snake carries away the person’s wine and meat, the person still sees the wine and meat.
To the person, there is only the sight of the wine and meat, yet these are not two sets of wine and meat, but merely one set of wine and meat.
When a snake is about to depart, one still perceives it as a person departing;
such is the inconceivable nature of the karmic formations within the snake’s belly.
Thus, although gold is absent, wood is still perceived; yet though wood is perceived, these are not two distinct substances.
Next, let us cite another matter.
It is simply a single substance of gold; those with merit see it as gold, while those with little merit see it as a snake.
Although two people perceive this single substance differently, despite the difference in perception, it remains but a single substance.
Question:
Since it is but a single substance, if one cuts through the snake, does one cut through the gold; and if one cuts through the gold, does one cut through the snake?
I ask this directly, yet I do not know how to answer.
Now, it is clear that although one may obtain the power to sever snakes, this does not mean one can sever gold; yet, if one cannot sever gold, one still severs snakes.
To say that obtaining the power to sever snakes means one immediately severs gold—this is the statement of our Great Master.
Why is this? It is like two people traveling together who see a piece of gold; they both yield to one another and thus do not take it, leaving it behind.
Later, another person comes along and sees that the piece of gold has become a snake; he immediately cuts it in two and departs.
Therefore it is said: "When two people are of one heart, their kindred power can sever metal. Thus, severing a snake is equivalent to severing metal.
As for not being able to sever metal yet severing a snake: it is because he did not originally perceive the metal; therefore, he could not sever the metal but severed the snake.
Question:
If severing the snake is equivalent to severing the gold, then burning away what is defiled should likewise burn away what is pure.
Explanation:
Furthermore, for this purpose it is said that cutting the snake is equivalent to cutting the gold, and burning the impure is equivalent to burning the pure.
Next, the primary fruits (maulaphala) are categorized by analogy with the fourfold sets of the preceding dependent fruits (niṣyandaphala).
Why is this? It was stated previously:

"There are two types of lands: those with two substances in one location, those with one substance in two locations, those with one substance in one location, and those with two substances in two locations."
Furthermore, it is said:
"two substances and one vision," "one substance and two visions," "one substance and one vision," and "two substances and two visions.

May these be analogized to the four permutations of two Buddhas in one place, one Buddha in two places, and so forth; and likewise to the four permutations of two Buddhas with one vision, one Buddha with two visions, and so forth?
The commentary states:

Since the fruits of retribution (*vipākaphala*) possess these two types of fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it follows that the primary fruits (*maulaphala*) likewise possess these two types of fourfold propositions.
Regarding these two types of fourfold propositions, the first four were composed by the Great Master, while the latter four were elucidated by the Scholar.
Regarding the statement "two Buddhas, one vision," this opens up two aspects of the fundamental and the trace:
this is the fundamental as the trace, and this is the trace as the fundamental.

As for the fundamental and the trace in terms of causes and conditions, if they are the fundamental and the trace in terms of causes and conditions, then they are not [the true] fundamental and the trace.

The "original" (hon) and the "trace" (jaku) constitute two aspects, yet that which is neither original nor trace constitutes a single locus; therefore, it is said that although the original and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one.
What is this inconceivable oneness?
Dharma Master Zhaolong Zhe established the formal argument.
Someone asked:
"The 'Inconceivable One' is singular; what is the name of that one thing?"
The commentary explains:
"One name is 'Right Nature' (samyaktva-niyāma).
The Great Master says:
It is not the nature of liberation. The true nature consists of five natures.
Among these five natures, four—namely, cause, causal cause, fruit, and resultant fruit—are the nature of conditions; the non-fruit is the true nature.
The Inconceivable One does not attain the Way; this is the True Nature (bhūtatathatā).
The Master said:
"Regarding the two aspects of origin and trace, Vairocana and Śākyamuni are neither origin nor trace; they are called the True Dharmakāya."
Although the original and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one; this constitutes two Buddhas in one place. As for one Buddha in two places:

the True Dharma is not the original or the trace, yet it constitutes one Buddha; being neither original nor trace, it constitutes the original and the trace as two places. Thus, while the original and the trace are one, they are inconceivably distinct.
Although previously the inconceivable was one, that one was an inconceivable one;
although now the inconceivable is one, that one is an inconceivable one. Thus it is said that "one Buddha is in two places."
"One Buddha in one place" does not mean that the provisional and ultimate Buddhas are located in separate provisional and ultimate places.
"Two Buddhas in two places" means that the provisional and ultimate Buddhas are situated in their respective provisional and ultimate places.
Next, the four propositions—“the two Buddhas are one vision,” and so forth—are explained. First, to distinguish “the two Buddhas are one vision”:

the fundamental and the manifested trace constitute the causal conditions of the fundamental and the trace; yet these causal conditions of the fundamental and the trace are themselves neither fundamental nor trace. Therefore, as previously stated, when the wise understand that ignorance and enlightenment are causal conditions, they realize their non-duality; thus, the two Buddhas are one vision.
Regarding "one Buddha and two manifestations": the true Dharmakāya is neither fundamental nor derivative, and thus is non-dual.
Why? Because the two conditions perceive the fundamental and the derivative as two, whereas the Dharmakāya has never been dual.
Regarding the conditions for perceiving the fundamental and the manifested: the Dharma-body has never possessed a distinction between fundamental and manifested;

therefore, this constitutes "one Buddha and two perspectives. As for "one Buddha and one perspective": the Dharma-body Buddha is neither fundamental nor manifested; because one perceives it by taking the Dharma-body as the condition, this constitutes "one Buddha and one perspective."
Regarding "the two Buddhas and the two visions": the Dharma-body is neither the fundamental nor the manifested; it is the fundamental and the manifested that respond to conditions.
Since the fundamental and the manifested respond to conditions, those conditions then perceive the fundamental and the manifested.
If the fundamental and the manifested did not respond to conditions, there would be no way for those conditions to perceive the fundamental and the manifested.

This is fundamentally because the original and the manifested respond to conditions; thus, through conditions, one perceives both the original and the manifested, resulting in two Buddhas and two perspectives.
Consequently, even regarding the ultimate fruit, there are likewise two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Next, two further sets of four propositions are combined to clarify both the primary and secondary fruits.
First, one set of four propositions will be explained. What are they?
This refers to: one Buddha in many places; many Buddhas in one place; one Buddha in one place; and many Buddhas in many places.

Regarding "one Buddha in one place," as clarified in the "Chapter on King Guṇa" of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Śākyamuni possesses a pure land located in the western direction called *Anabhibhūta* (Invincible).
This means that a single Śākyamuni exists in both pure and impure realms.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Śākyamuni has both impure lands and pure lands. Since Śākyamuni’s impure land possesses pure lands, Amitābha’s pure land likewise possesses impure lands; therefore, it is said that one Buddha resides in many places.

Regarding many Buddhas being in one place: this is as clarified in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, where the Buddhas of the ten directions are shown to be together in the Sahā world, and also as when the five Buddhas appeared together in the room of Śraddhālakṣaṇa.
Regarding "one Buddha in one place," Śākyamuni is in the eastern direction while Amitābha dwells in the western land.
Regarding "many Buddhas in many places," this refers to the Buddhas of the ten directions residing in the lands of the ten directions.
Next, there are four further propositions: namely, one Buddha in two places; two Buddhas in one place; one Buddha in one place; and two Buddhas in two places. Regarding "one Buddha in two places":
Śākyamuni is identical to Vairocana, and Vairocana is identical to Śākyamuni, thus they constitute one Buddha;
yet the Jetavana Grove differs in being either pure or impure, thus they constitute two places.
Regarding "two Buddhas in one place": Śākyamuni and Sāṃbhogakāya (Sānabuddha) are two Buddhas; although Jetavana is both pure and impure, it is but a single Jetavana, thus constituting one place.
Regarding "one Buddha in one place": the fundamental and the manifested are one Buddha, and the pure and impure Jetavana constitute one place.
"Two Buddhas and two places" refers to the two Buddhas of the original and the manifested, and the two places of the pure and the defiled.
However, these four phrases are difficult to explain; for now, they have been established as topical headings in this manner.
This shall be explained in detail later in the eighth assembly.
A brief clarification of the meaning of the "lands" (*kṣetra*) is thus concluded.
Now, I shall address the four preceding questions in general.
Why is this? One school clarifies the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
If it were not through dependent origination, the meaning of manifestation would not be established, and one would be refuting the [opponent's] doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is clear that since all present conditions are conditions, one and two, or two and one, may serve as conditions; but how can one and one, or two and two, function as conditions?
It is like the initial striking of a lute: its existence depends on another, yet that "existence" is itself self-existent, and its non-existence is itself self-non-existent.
If it exists inherently, it exists because of its own existence; if it does not exist inherently, it does not exist because of its own non-existence.
To have existence or non-existence while being independent of causes and conditions—how could each of these, taken individually or in pairs, constitute a causal condition?
Furthermore, let us clarify the fourfold formulation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the fourfold formulation regarding causes and conditions.

Regarding the fourfold formulation of causes and conditions: it is neither "fourfold formulation" nor "not fourfold formulation," and it is neither "not fourfold formulation" nor "fourfold formulation."
These four phrases are all causes and conditions; this is the general explanation.
Next is the specific explanation.
The previous general [explanation] was vertical and dense, whereas the present specific [explanation] is horizontal and sparse.
To clarify separately that all four permutations are dependent origination: because of one and two there are two and one; because of two and one there are one and two.
If the dependent origination of one and two and two and one is the same as the dependent origination of one and one and two and two?
The commentary states:
Because of two-ones, one-ones arise; how then could there be a single "one-one"?
Because of two-ones, there are two-ones; thus, because of two-ones, there are one-ones.

Since the one-and-one arises from the two-and-one, and the two-and-one also arises from the one-and-one, then the one-and-one is caused by the two-and-two, and the one-and-one is caused by the one-and-one.

Since the two-and-two arises from the one-and-two, and the one-and-two also arises from the two-and-two, then the two-and-two is caused by the one-and-two, and the one-and-two is caused by the two-and-two.
Thus, all four propositions are dependent origination.

These four propositions of dependent origination—and the dependent origination of the four propositions—are neither four propositions, nor non-four propositions, nor not-non-four propositions; they are ultimately pure.
Although the above clarifies these four propositions, there has never been a single school that has explained them in this way.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Subhūti addressed the devaputras:
'I have nothing to say; there are no words with which to speak.'"
"This means that in discourse there is nothing to be discoursed upon, and in speech there is nothing to be spoken.

Now it is likewise so: though there are immeasurable fourfold sets (*catuṣkoṭi*), they have never been fourfold sets; yet these immeasurable fourfold sets are, while being immeasurable, a single one; and though it is a single one, it is immeasurable.
The One Immeasurable is immeasurable yet one; though there is nothing to be said, it speaks.
Though it speaks, there is nothing spoken; when expanded, it pervades and fills the Dharma-realm; when contracted, it merges into non-existence.
Though it is condensed, there is nothing that is not contained within it.
It must simply pass through me in this manner: it cannot be fragmented, nor can it be indistinct.
To be fragmented is to fall into the attainment of something; to be indistinct makes it impossible to understand.
Now, for the time being, we have moved from the distinct to the indistinct, and from the indistinct back to the distinct.
This is a brief clarification of the meaning of the Pure Land;
thus, two of the four points of meaning have been roughly concluded.
Now, for the third time, we clarify the teaching of the Dharma-gate.
The previous clarification of the places where the transformation-masters acted constitutes the primary and secondary realms, as well as the subjective and objective aspects.

Where there is a transformer, there is that which is transformed; where there is that which is transformed, there is a transformer. Thus, the primary and secondary realms are fully endowed with the causal conditions of the subjective and objective.
What is the purpose of this transformation-master and this place of transformation?
It is to establish teachings for the sake of those to be transformed.
Therefore, the third section now clarifies the gateway of teaching.
Within the gateway of the teachings, there are generally three propositions:
first, the subject and object; second, cause and effect; and third, the partial and the complete, and the permanent and the impermanent.
Although the Master clearly elucidates these three types, they are all interconnected; this critical analysis and deliberation merely preserves the general intent.
The Great Master said:

"The meaning of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*) is the most extensive; cause and effect occupy the middle ground; and the meanings of the 'half' and 'full' [teachings], as well as permanence and impermanence, are the most restricted.
Nevertheless, for now we shall clarify the meaning of subject and object, further opening this into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*)."
The first is "the agent but not the object," which concerns the meaning of the constant and the inconstant, and the half and the full.
This shall be explained in detail later in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; for now, I shall provide a summary by grasping the main framework to distinguish its essential points.
The first is "capable but not the locus"; the second is "the locus but not capable"; the third is "both capable and the locus"; and the fourth is "neither capable nor the locus.

Regarding what is called "capable but not the locus": when one adds [new] teachings to those already received, there is no causal condition for attaining awakening; this is termed "capable but not the locus."

Regarding that which cannot be accomplished: there may be sentient beings who awaken to the Way upon seeing leaves fall, or become sages by observing flowers wither; if the Tathāgata does not employ such teachings for them, it is called "that which cannot be accomplished."

Regarding "both the capable and the object": there is the teaching that is capable of acting upon others, and there are the conditions that are the objects of its action. The teaching is the condition for the teaching, and the conditions are the conditions for the teaching; the teaching and the conditions correspond to one another, and the conditions correspond to the teaching and the teaching corresponds to the conditions. Because they harmonize so as to enable sentient beings to attain the Way, it is called "both the capable and the object."

"Neither that which can act nor that which is acted upon" means there is no Tathāgata who can exercise the teaching, nor is there any sentient being who is the object of that conditioning; therefore, it is called "neither that which can act nor that which is acted upon.
Question:
For what reason are these four phrases elucidated?
The commentary states:
Although these four propositions have been clarified, here we shall distinguish the teaching by focusing specifically on the proposition that is both agent and object.
For what purpose is this teaching elucidated?
The Mingjiao [Master] intends to address the conditions [of the teaching]; therefore, he now distinguishes it according to the second phrase, which is both the agent and the object.
Although it is both the agent and the object, for the time being, he clarifies the teaching as that which is capable of acting upon others.
The fourth section following this clarifies the objects [of the teaching] that are addressed;
now, this section clarifies the teaching itself that is capable of addressing them.
Question:
Question: Are the teachings bestowed by the two Buddhas, Śākyamuni and Śikhin, the same or different?
Answer: It is explained that the teachings bestowed by the two Buddhas are the same.
Question:
Since the two Buddhas are distinct, how can their teachings be identical?
Explanation:
Although the two teachers differ, their administration of the teachings is equally for the purpose of manifesting the Way.
Since the manifestation of the Way is not different, the principle of their administration of the teachings is the same. Why is this so?
The Path is that which is revealed, and the teaching is that which expresses it; since the Path revealed is without difference, the teachings that express it are identical.
This being so for these two Buddhas, it is likewise for all Buddhas of the ten directions.
For what purpose do the Buddhas of the ten directions bestow their teachings?
It is to manifest the Way, which is identical in all cases.
Because they manifest the Way, the meaning of their teachings is the same.
Next, to clarify that the teachings of the two Buddhas are identical: they are identical in their elucidation of the Dharma-gate of cause and effect.
Although the teachings of the two Buddhas are immeasurable, they do not transcend the Dharma-gate of cause and effect.
The Dharma-gate of cause and effect is likewise for all the Buddhas of the ten directions; it does not transcend the Dharma-gate of cause and effect.

The teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions do not transcend the Dharma-gate of cause and effect; now, this Dharma-gate of cause and effect encompasses the entirety of the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Since it is clear that the Dharma-gate of cause and effect is identical, the teachings of these two Buddhas are not different.

However, this cause and effect is not the cause and effect of the six causes and five effects of the Sautrāntikas, nor the simultaneous cause and effect or the asynchronous cause and effect of the Śāstrins, nor the cause and effect of the four conditions and three causes.
These so-called causes and effects do not possess the true meaning of cause and effect.

Previously, the Master [Nāgārjuna] refuted these notions of cause and effect in the "Examination of Causes and Effects" chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, clarifying that they are neither such causes nor such effects.
Examining this cause, one finds nothing that is not a cause; seeking this effect, one finds nothing that is not an effect.

Having thus concluded the discussion on such causes and effects, one finally attains clarity regarding the conditions of the present moment: the conditionality of conditions, and the mutual non-obstruction between cause and effect and cause and cause.
They may occur simultaneously, or they may occur at different times.

There are causes and conditions that are simultaneous; causes and conditions that are at different times; causes and conditions that are both simultaneous and not simultaneous; and causes and conditions that are at different times and yet not at different times.

Although they are not simultaneous, they are simultaneous; although they are not different times, they are different times. This must always be understood through the analogy of an echo in a valley or a reflection in a clear mirror.

It is necessary to first refute the causality of others before one can clarify the causal conditions and the causes and effects of the present; only then does the meaning of causality become established.
Therefore, the two Buddhas equally elucidate causality.
Question:
Are the two Buddhas clarifying cause and effect together?
Explanation:
The two Buddhas equally clarify the principle of cause and effect, each possessing the meanings of both distinction and non-distinction, as well as non-distinction and distinction.
Regarding Śākyamuni’s distinction and non-distinction: there is one cause of prajñā and one fruit of sarvajñā; there is one cause of buddha-nature and one fruit of nirvāṇa.

Regarding "the non-differentiation and differentiation of Śākyamuni": the single cause of *prajñā* is opened up into immeasurable causes, namely the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) shared by the three vehicles;
the single fruit of *sarvajñatā* is opened up into immeasurable fruits, namely the fruit of *sarvajñatā*, the fruit of *bodhi*, and the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the meaning of the distinction and non-distinction, as well as the non-distinction within distinction, of *vimala-śānti* (pure tranquility): practicing the single cause that transcends the world and attaining the fruit of the single *dharmadhātu* constitutes the meaning of non-distinction.

The causes—the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages—as well as the perfect fruits—the ten oceans of worlds, the ocean of great and small marks, and the manifestation of bodies such as the original and the trace—are precisely the meaning of non-differentiation within differentiation.

This refers to the fact that each of the two Buddhas possesses both the meaning of difference and non-difference; therefore, it is clear that the two Buddhas are identical in terms of cause and effect.
As for what is called "difference," Śākyamuni primarily elucidates the meaning of difference within non-difference.

The meanings of "bundling" and "scattering" clarify that there is one cause, which is *prajñā*, and one fruit, which is *sarvajñā*. This does not constitute the meaning of the "ten-tens" clarifications.

If this is the meaning of the non-differentiation of differentiation within the many *sāmbhogakāya* manifestations, then it encompasses the meanings of scattering and bundling, the ten-tens clarifications, the ten faiths and ten stages, and so forth, up to the two hundred questions of the Bodhisattva Samantamati and the two thousand answers of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra—wherein a single sentence is answered with ten sentences—and even up to the oceans of the ten Buddha-worlds and the oceans of large and small marks; therefore, this is the meaning of the non-differentiation of differentiation.
This is the meaning of the similarities and differences between the two Buddha-teachings.
Although the gateways of the two Buddha-teachings are thus shown to be manifold, they do not transcend cause and effect; therefore, both Buddhas equally elucidate cause and effect.
The Great Master has always said:
"The two Buddhas equally clarify cause and effect, yet their clarifications of cause and effect are not the same.

Regarding the statement that the two Buddhas equally clarify cause and effect: Śākyamuni is the one who transforms; he cultivated causes that are neither arising nor ceasing in the past, and has now attained a fruit that is neither interrupted nor eternal.
Since Śākyamuni’s capacity for transformation is thus, so too is that of Vairocana.
Through Vairocana’s capacity for transformation, he cultivated causes that are neither arising nor ceasing in the past, and has now attained fruits that are neither interrupted nor eternal.
Those transformed by Śākyamuni currently practice causes that are neither arising nor ceasing, and will in the future attain fruits that are neither interrupted nor eternal.

Since it is so for those transformed by Śākyamuni, it is likewise for those transformed by Vairocana: they currently practice causes that are neither arising nor ceasing, and will in the future attain fruits that are neither interrupted nor eternal.

Therefore, regarding the two Buddhas whose meanings of cause and effect are both identical and yet different: Śākyamuni’s capacity for transformation fully clarifies both cause and effect, whereas Vairocana’s capacity for transformation clarifies the effect but not the cause.
Those transformed by Vairocana fully clarify both cause and effect, whereas those transformed by Śākyamuni clarify only the cause and not the effect.

To say that Śākyamuni’s transformative teaching fully clarifies both cause and effect means that his teaching clarifies that one is currently an ordinary person who, by practicing the cause, attains the fruit.

Generally, there are two kinds of clarifications regarding causes: clarifying the past causes, such as the practice of the six perfections; and clarifying the present, such as leaving the city to study the Way and undergoing six years of asceticism. Because both the causes and effects of these two lifetimes are fully elucidated, this is what is meant by "clarifying the cause and discerning the effect. Attaining perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree is precisely the discernment of the effect; therefore, it is said that Śākyamuni’s capacity for transformation fully elucidates both cause and effect.

Regarding the statement that Vairocana’s capacity for transformation clarifies only the fruit and not the cause: the teachings of Vairocana do not clarify the causal practices through which Vairocana is able to manifest transformation.

Why is this? They do not clarify past causal practices, nor do they clarify present causal practices; rather, from the initial attainment of Bodhicitta by Vairocana, they clarify the two fruits of the environment and its inhabitants. The environmental fruit consists of the ten lands, and the fruit of the inhabitants consists of the ocean of the names of the ten Buddhas. Therefore, Vairocana’s capacity for transformation clarifies only the fruit and does not clarify the cause.

Regarding "those transformed by Vairocana who fully understand the cause and effect of practice": those transformed by Vairocana cultivate the causes such as the ten faiths and the ten stages, thereby attaining the fruit of the inconceivable ocean of marks of the Great and Small Vehicles; they practice the cause that transcends the world and attain the fruit of the Dharma-realm. Therefore, it is said that those transformed by Vairocana fully understand the cause of practice and the attainment of the fruit.

Śākyamuni’s transformation [of beings] clarifies only the cultivation of causes and does not distinguish the attainment of results; therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The bodhisattva, by means of the dharma of non-abiding, dwells within prajñā and fulfills the myriad practices."

This passage clarifies only the causes, such as the practice of prajñāpāramitā, and does not clarify the attainment of the fruit, sarvajñatā; therefore, those transformed by Śākyamuni possess only the cause and not the fruit.

However, these four propositions have been handed down from the Master of the Mountain; they represent an ancient interpretation of this school that is inherently difficult to grasp. Although later generations may be able to recite these words, they truly do not understand their underlying meaning.
Now, let me pose several questions for consideration.

Why? For it has already been stated that that which is transformed by Śāntamati practices the causes—the ten stages of faith and the ten bhūmis—and attains the fruit of the inconceivable ocean of marks of both the Great and the Small Vehicles; it practices causes that transcend the world and attains the fruit of the Dharma-realm.
How is this known? How is it known that the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth are the causes manifested by Vairocana,
while the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) and the ocean of qualities are the fruits manifested by Vairocana?
Later, in the section on the cycle of cause and effect, he likewise raises this objection:

"In the textual passages of this sutra’s seven locations and eight assemblies, where is it stated that the ten faiths and ten stages are the causes transformed by Śākyamuni, and the ocean of marks and signs is the fruit transformed by Vairocana?"
The subsequent cycle of cause and effect is also subject to this same critique.

Within the textual passages of this scripture’s seven locations and eight assemblies, at what point does the path transcending the world serve as the cause for those to be transformed, and where does the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) serve as the fruit for those to be transformed?

Furthermore, how can one know that the ten levels of faith and the ten abodes are not the causes for Śākyamuni’s transformation, and that the ocean of marks and signs of the Great and Small Vehicles are not the fruits of Śākyamuni’s transformation?
How can one know that the transcendence of the world is not the cause for Śākyamuni’s transformation, and that the Dharma-realm is not the fruit of his transformation?
Furthermore, there is one point of censure:

if you say that the ten faiths and the ten stages are the causes transformed by Vairocana, and the marks and signs of the great and small are the fruits transformed by Vairocana, then should these fruits of the marks and signs of the great and small be attained in the present through Vairocana’s transformation?

If it were claimed that those transformed by Vairocana do not attain the fruit of the ocean of marks and signs, yet Vairocana nonetheless preaches for the sake of the bodhisattvas that these present bodhisattvas cultivate the causes and take up the fruit—how would this differ from the transformation of Śākyamuni?
Śākyamuni also taught the fruits such as nirvāṇa and sarvajñā for the sake of the bodhisattvas; now these bodhisattvas clearly take these fruits by means of the causes.

If this is so, since there is no difference between the beings transformed by the two Buddhas, how can it be determined that those transformed by Śākyamuni possess only the cause but not the fruit, while those transformed by Vairocana possess both cause and fruit?
If one were to say that those transformed by Vairocana have already attained the fruit of the ocean of major and minor marks, then all bodhisattvas would be Buddhas.
Why is this? Because the fruit of the ocean of major and minor marks belongs to the Tathāgata’s own ocean of major and minor marks.

Once these bodhisattvas have attained this fruit, they would already be Buddhas; why then would they need to further practice the causes for transcending the world in order to attain the dharma-realm?
This twofold objection regarding the proliferation of meanings is difficult to resolve.
The reason it cannot be easily understood is that because the teachers of old have used such terminology, it is difficult to comprehend; it does not involve other matters.
Nevertheless, the meaning and characteristics of the cause and fruit of the two Buddhas are extremely difficult to perceive.
It was previously stated that Śākyamuni is able to possess both cause and effect, yet his cause is not the effect; whereas Vairocana possesses only the effect and has no cause.
What is the intention behind clarifying this distinction between their causes and effects?
To clarify the meaning of this composition, the Great Master Fèn stated:
"The reason for elucidating these four lines concerning cause and effect is to distinguish the mutual relationship between the two Buddhas as subject and object."

The Śākyamuni who transforms others possesses the clarity of cause and effect, and the Vairocana who is transformed by him likewise possesses the clarity of cause and effect. This constitutes the relationship between the agent and the object; it is not that the agent exists without the object being established, nor that the object exists without the agent being established. The agent is the object of the agent, and the object is the agent of the object; thus, both this agent and this object are fully endowed with cause and effect.

Although both possess cause and effect, they each embody the principle of a single cause and a single effect; thus, Śākyamuni is able to fully clarify cause and effect, and Vairocana likewise fully clarifies cause and effect.

Regarding the second phrase concerning the combination of characteristics: if it is said that the emanations of Vairocana possess only the fruit but not the cause, while those emanated by Śākyamuni possess only the cause but not the fruit, this too constitutes the relationship between the agent and the object.

Without the subject (the "able"), there is no way to clarify the object (the "so"); without the object, there is no way to clarify the subject. Since the fruit of the subject-object relationship encompasses both the causal subject and the causal object, and the causal subject-object relationship encompasses both the resultant subject and the resultant object, this relationship of subject and object also carries the meaning of being simultaneously cause and effect. Therefore, the "ability" of Vairocana is solely the fruit and not the cause, while the "object" of Śākyamuni is solely the cause and not the fruit.

Regarding the third phrase, "the mutual inclusion of characteristics": Śākyamuni’s capacity encompasses the capacity of Vairocana; Śākyamuni’s capacity consists of the two meanings within one, while Vairocana’s capacity consists of the one meaning within two. This duality is the "one-and-two," and this unity is the "two-and-one. This original is the trace-original, and this trace is the original-trace. Because of the original-trace, there is "one-and-two"; because of the trace-original, there is "two-and-one. "One-and-two" includes "two-and-one," and "two-and-one" includes "one-and-two. Because the original-trace includes the trace-original and the trace-original includes the original-trace, Śākyamuni’s capacity fully elucidates both cause and fruit, whereas Vairocana’s capacity pertains only to the cause and not the fruit.
The Great Master has spoken only these words.
Now I ask further:
for what purpose are these four phrases explained as the mutual integration of cause and effect?
The commentary states:
There are two meanings.
First, it clarifies that the subject and object of the two Buddhas are mutually interpenetrating.
Since it is explained that Śākyamuni’s capacity for transformation possesses both cause and effect, it is revealed that Vairocana’s capacity for transformation is likewise;
since it is explained that Vairocana’s capacity for transformation has only the fruit and no cause, it is revealed that Śākyamuni’s capacity for transformation is likewise.
The two Buddhas constitute two phrases, yet each merely manifests a single meaning; thus, "one" and "two" differ.
As it is with the transformer (the Buddha), so it is with the transformed (the sentient beings); this principle is easy to understand.
Second, there is the desire to obliterate the meanings of subject and object, cause and effect, and original and trace.

In this regard, Śākyamuni’s original and trace aspects are "one and two," while Vairocana’s trace and original aspects are "two and one. The original is not the trace, and the trace is not the original; "one and two" are not two, and "two and one" are not one; subject and object are not object, and object and subject are not subject. Thus, they are neither one nor two, neither original nor trace, and are ultimately pure.
This is what is meant by the meaning of "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya).
To further explain the meaning of the preceding phrase: what is it?

Regarding the statement that the preceding [section on] Śākyamuni’s capacity for transformation describes only the fruit and not the cause, while those being transformed possess both cause and fruit: this clarifies that this sutra, at its inception, speaks only of the two fruits—the environment and the body—of Śākyamuni. The ten Buddha-lands are the environmental fruit (the *āśraya-phala*), and the ten Buddha-world-oceans are the personal fruit (the *sambhoga-phala*); it does not, however, clarify the causes of Śākyamuni’s capacity for transformation.

If this refers to that which is transformed by Vairocana, the previously explained five stages—namely the ten levels of faith and the ten bhūmis—are the causes of what is transformed, while the ocean of marks and signs is the fruit of what is transformed; this constitutes one cycle clarifying the meaning of the causes and fruits of that which is transformed.
Next, there is another cycle that clarifies the causes and effects of those to be transformed, namely, the cause of transcending the world and the fruit of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Between these two cycles of cause and effect, the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Xingqi pin*) concludes the preceding section and gives rise to the subsequent one.

Regarding the "concluding the preceding": first, the five stages of cause were clarified; next, the fruit of the ocean of marks and characteristics of the Great and Small Vehicles was clarified. The "Nature-Arising" chapter then subsumes these causes and fruits, returning them to the meaning of the single true nature that is neither cause nor fruit.

Regarding "arising after" (*shenghou*): it is by means of that which is neither cause nor effect that one first comes to clarify cause and effect; this carries the meaning of function emerging from essence.

It is by means of that which is not a cause that one first clarifies the supramundane cause, and by means of that which is not an effect that one first distinguishes the fruition of the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" concludes the preceding section by introducing what follows.
Now I ask:

how can it be known that these ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and so forth—the causes and the ocean of marks of the Great and Small Vehicles—are the effects produced by Vairocana?
How can one know that these are the effects produced [by him] rather than the causes [produced] by him as the transformer?
The commentary states:

The reason we know that the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the ten stages of the bodhisattva path (*daśa-bhūmi*) are the causes for those to be transformed is that it clarifies how the Tathāgata encourages sentient beings who are to be transformed by means of such causes, urging them to practice these causes and making it clear: "If you can practice these causes, you will certainly attain Buddhahood."
Thus, one knows that this cause and effect are the cause and effect manifested by Samantabhadra.
The Great Master said:
"This, then, implies that the object of transformation possesses the sense of 'long-term persistence' (chang-you) as well."
Why is this? Because that which is transformed by Śānta includes the cause of the transformer, yet it cannot include the object of transformation.
To say that the cause of the transformed includes the cause of the transformer clarifies that the practice of the transformed attains the fruit through these various causes.
One should know that the Śānta (the Tranquil One) can transform these causes of such practices so as to bring about their results.
Objection:
If the causes of the transformed are inclusive of the causes of the transformer, then the results of the transformed should also be inclusive of the results of the transformer.
If the causes of the transformed (*nirmeya*) were to include the causes of the transformer (*nirmātr*), then the effects of the transformer should likewise include the effects of the transformed.
Explanation:
It is not possible for the effects of the transformer to include the effects of the transformed.

Why is this? It is because one wishes to praise how the results obtained from the distinct causes currently practiced by those transformed by Vairocana are realized; therefore, the fruit of the transformer cannot be conflated with the fruit of the transformed.
Objection:
It is evident that the transformed being attains a distinct fruit, yet does not attain the fruit of the transformer combined with the fruit of the transformed.
Likewise, the transformer must also have a distinct cause; he cannot obtain the cause of the transformed combined with his own cause as the transformer.
The commentary states:
If they were combined and integrated, they would constitute a single meaning.
Now, since each presents a distinct meaning, they are not the same.
Question:
For what reason can a cause be accompanied by its effect, yet an effect cannot be accompanied by its cause?
Explanation:
There are cases where [the principle] applies and cases where it does not; they cannot be treated as one and the same.
Furthermore, that which was not yet fully understood shall be explained again.
Next, another question is asked:
Why is it that those transformed by Śākyamuni possess only the cause but not the fruit, whereas those transformed by Vairocana possess both cause and fruit?
The explanation states:

due to the distinctions between purity and defilement, as well as sharpness and dullness of faculties, those transformed by Śākyamuni reside in a defiled land with dull faculties; therefore, they practice the cause but do not immediately attain the fruit.
In the pure lands manifested by Vairocana, those with sharp faculties obtain the fruit immediately upon performing the causal practice;
this is the general judgment.
However, in a detailed analysis, those transformed by Śākyamuni do not obtain the fruit while still in the causal stage, yet it is not that they lack the complete cause and fruit.
The causes and conditions manifested by Vairocana possess both cause and effect; it is not the case that they lack cause, nor is it the case that what is not a cause is not an effect.
Why is this? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are two ways in which Śākyamuni turns the wheel of Dharma:..."
Within the Secret Dharma Wheel, there are those who attain non-arising and those who manifest Buddhahood in this very body.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "Upon hearing the teaching of Prajñā, one attains perfect enlightenment in the present."

If that which is emanated by Śākyamuni has causes but no results, then since there are both causes and results, it follows that what is emanated by Vairocana possesses both causes and results; yet there is also that which has causes but no results.
Question:
If this is so, why was this explanation composed?
The answer states:
This is the general judgment. *Huayan youyi* (The Intent of Wandering through the Avataṃsaka).
